title: 9 Questions Before Choosing Managed WiFi
summary: Discover 9 critical questions to ask before choosing managed WiFi for your multifamily or student housing property. Evaluate vendors and protect your NOI.
body_text: Choosing a managed WiFi partner for your multifamily or student housing property is one of the more consequential infrastructure decisions you'll make. The right network drives resident satisfaction, protects your NOI and positions your asset for long-term value. The wrong one creates support headaches, locks you into contracts that don't serve your interests and leaves property teams fielding complaints. This article walks through nine questions that cut through vendor marketing and surface what matters for your property economics and operations. Elauwit Connection has deployed networks across 38,000+ units in 25 states, and these questions reflect what experienced operators ask before signing. Quick guide: 9 key questions for managed WiFi vendor evaluation Who owns the network infrastructure after installation? Determines long-term control and asset value What does resident support look like, and who handles it? Separates marketing claims from operational reality How does the contract handle early termination? Reveals vendor flexibility and risk allocation What coverage gaps exist in your deployment plan? Identifies where complaints will originate How do you handle move-in day and mass onboarding? Tests whether the network can handle real-world surges What financing or capital structure options exist? Aligns network investment with your asset strategy How do you approach network upgrades and technology refresh? Determines whether the network stays current or becomes a liability What NOI impact can I model from this deployment? Grounds the decision in actual property economics Who is accountable when something goes wrong? The question that reveals everything How we developed these evaluation criteria These questions come from two decades of deploying managed networks across conventional multifamily, student housing and mixed-use communities. We've seen what separates vendors who deliver from those who disappear after installation. Ownership structure clarity: You need to know whether you're building an asset or renting one, because the answer affects your cap rate, your flexibility and your exit options. Resident support accountability: The support model determines whether your leasing team fields internet complaints or focuses on leasing. Contract transparency: Early termination clauses, auto-renewal terms and exclusivity provisions reveal how vendors think about the relationship. Coverage engineering: Dead zones in amenity areas or inconsistent in-unit performance generate resident complaints regardless of marketing claims. Onboarding capacity: Student housing move-in day and lease-up surges expose whether the network architecture can handle real-world demand. Financial alignment: Capital expenditure versus operating expense models affect how the investment appears on your books and your ability to scale across a portfolio. Technology lifecycle planning: Networks that don't evolve become liabilities, so understanding the vendor's refresh approach matters for long-term value. The 9 questions every property owner should ask 1. Who owns the network infrastructure after installation? This question determines whether you're building an asset that contributes to property value or simply paying for a service. Some vendors retain ownership of all installed equipment. Others transfer ownership to you. The distinction affects your balance sheet, your flexibility to switch providers and your property's long-term value. Elauwit Connection offers both structures: Managed Service where you own the network, and Network-as-a-Service where Elauwit owns the infrastructure with $0 upfront capital for the core build. The right choice depends on your capital strategy and how you want the asset to appear on your books. Why ownership matters for your asset Cap rate impact: Owner-owned infrastructure contributes to asset value at sale, while service-only arrangements don't add tangible value to the property. Provider flexibility: If you own the network, you can change operators without starting from zero on infrastructure. Revenue control: Ownership often means you control resident pricing and keep a larger share of recurring revenue. Portfolio consistency: For multi-property operators, understanding ownership across your portfolio affects how you model value and manage assets. Ownership question pros and cons Pros Cons Clarifies long-term asset value contribution Requires understanding your capital strategy before evaluating Reveals vendor flexibility on structure Some vendors only offer one model, limiting options Surfaces hidden equipment lease terms May require deeper financial analysis to compare models 2. What does resident support look like, and who handles it? Every managed WiFi vendor claims to handle support. The question is what that means in practice. When a resident has a connectivity issue at 11 p.m., who picks up the phone? How long do they wait? Does the issue get resolved, or does the resident call your leasing office the next morning? Elauwit Connection answers calls from real humans in less than 30 seconds, 24/7. That's not a marketing claim. It's a measured operational standard that keeps support calls off your property team's desk. Support model features to evaluate Response time commitments: Ask for actual average response times, not just "24/7 support" claims that may route to voicemail. Escalation paths: Understand what happens when an issue requires on-site intervention and who coordinates that. Property team involvement: Determine whether your leasing staff will be pulled into support tickets or whether the provider handles end-to-end. Support question pros and cons Pros Cons Directly affects resident satisfaction and reviews Hard to verify claims without references or trial period Determines whether leasing team stays focused on leasing Support quality can vary by region or time of day Separates vendors with real operations from resellers Requires asking for specific metrics, not just testimonials 3. How does the contract handle early termination? Contracts reveal how vendors think about the relationship. Restrictive early termination clauses, automatic renewal provisions and exclusivity requirements signal a vendor who relies on lock-in rather than performance. Ask specifically: What happens if you need to sell the property? What if the service doesn't perform as promised? What are the actual costs to exit before the term ends? Contract terms to scrutinize Termination penalties: Some vendors charge the full remaining contract value. Others pro-rate or offer reasonable exit provisions. Auto-renewal terms: Understand how much notice you need to give and what happens if you miss the window. Assignment provisions: If you sell the property, can the contract transfer to the new owner, or are you liable for the remainder? Contract question pros and cons Pros Cons Surfaces vendor confidence in their own service quality Requires legal review to understand full implications Reveals flexibility for portfolio-scale operators Shorter terms may come with higher monthly costs Protects against being trapped with underperforming service Some contract flexibility depends on property size and deal structure 4. What coverage gaps exist in your deployment plan? Marketing materials show coverage maps with consistent signal throughout the property. Reality is more nuanced. Amenity areas, parking structures, outdoor spaces and certain unit layouts present engineering challenges. A vendor who acknowledges these challenges and addresses them in the deployment plan is more credible than one who promises perfection. Elauwit Connection designs networks specifically for multifamily communities, accounting for the construction materials, unit density and common area layouts that create coverage challenges in residential properties. Coverage evaluation features Amenity area coverage: Pools, fitness centers, clubhouses and coworking spaces need reliable connectivity for resident satisfaction. In-unit consistency: Ask how the network handles units with challenging layouts, thick walls or significant distance from access points. Roaming performance: Residents expect their devices to stay connected as they move through the property without dropping calls or buffering. Coverage question pros and cons Pros Cons Identifies where resident complaints will originate before deployment Requires site survey to validate, not just vendor assurances Tests vendor's engineering depth versus sales positioning Perfect coverage may require additional infrastructure investment Surfaces hidden costs for full-property coverage Some coverage limitations are physics, not vendor capability 5. How do you handle move-in day and mass onboarding? Student housing properties face a specific challenge: thousands of residents arriving within days, each bringing five or more devices, all expecting immediate connectivity. Conventional multifamily properties face similar surges during lease-up. The network architecture needs to handle these peak loads without degrading performance. Ask vendors how their onboarding process works. Can residents pre-register before arrival? How quickly can they connect on move-in day? What happens when 500 people try to activate simultaneously? Onboarding features to evaluate Pre-registration capability: Allowing residents to set up accounts before move-in reduces day-one chaos and support volume. Device handling: Students and residents bring multiple devices. The network needs to handle this density without bottlenecks. Self-service activation: The less staff involvement required for activation, the better for property operations during peak periods. Onboarding question pros and cons Pros Cons Critical for student housing where move-in is concentrated May require coordination with property team on communication Reduces support ticket volume during highest-stress periods Pre-registration requires resident data sharing and privacy considerations Tests whether vendor has experience with your property type Onboarding process quality varies by vendor and property type 6. What financing or capital structure options exist? Network infrastructure requires investment. How that investment is structured affects your capital allocation, your monthly cash flow and how the asset appears on your books. Vendors who offer only one structure may not align with your portfolio strategy. Elauwit Connection offers flexible structures: owner-funded builds for maximum yield and Network-as-a-Service with $0 upfront capital. The right model depends on your capital constraints, your timeline and how you want to structure the economics. Financing features to consider Capital versus operating expense: Understand whether the investment appears as CapEx or OpEx and how that affects your financial reporting. Upfront versus recurring costs: Some models require significant upfront investment. Others spread costs over time with predictable monthly fees. Revenue share structures: If you're collecting fees from residents, understand how revenue is split between you and the provider. Financing question pros and cons Pros Cons Aligns network investment with portfolio capital strategy Requires financial modeling to compare structures Surfaces vendors willing to work with your constraints Lower upfront cost may mean less ownership control Enables deployment timing that matches development schedules Some structures only available above certain unit counts 7. How do you approach network upgrades and technology refresh? Network technology evolves. WiFi 6 replaced WiFi 5. WiFi 7 is emerging. Resident bandwidth expectations grow every year. A network that meets current needs may become a liability in three years if there's no plan for technology refresh. Ask vendors how they handle upgrades. Is technology refresh included in ongoing service? Who pays for equipment replacement? How do they manage upgrades in occupied buildings with minimal disruption? Technology refresh features Upgrade inclusion: Some service models include technology refresh. Others treat upgrades as separate projects requiring new investment. Disruption management: Upgrades in occupied properties require planning to minimize impact on residents. Future-proofing approach: Understand whether the infrastructure being installed today can support tomorrow's technology or will require replacement. Technology question pros and cons Pros Cons Prevents network from becoming outdated liability Upgrade commitments add to total cost of ownership Shows vendor's long-term thinking versus short-term sales Future technology needs are difficult to predict precisely Protects asset value as technology standards evolve Some upgrade paths depend on initial infrastructure choices 8. What NOI impact can I model from this deployment? Managed WiFi should contribute to property economics, not just resident satisfaction. The question is whether you can model that contribution with real numbers. Ask vendors for specific examples: What NOI improvement have similar properties seen? What assumptions drive those projections? Industry research shows 200-300 basis points of NOI improvement for properties with managed connectivity (NMHC, 2025). At a 5.5% cap rate, that translates to meaningful asset value creation. But the specific impact depends on your property, your market and your execution. NOI modeling features Revenue contribution: Understand what resident fees you can charge and what your share of that revenue will be. Operational savings: Quantify the reduction in property team time spent on connectivity complaints. Asset value impact: Model how improved NOI translates to property value at your market cap rate. NOI question pros and cons Pros Cons Grounds decision in property economics rather than features Projections depend on assumptions that may not match your property Enables comparison across vendors using consistent metrics Actual results vary by market, property type and execution Separates marketing claims from verifiable outcomes Requires financial analysis capability to validate projections 9. Who is accountable when something goes wrong? This question reveals everything. When the network goes down, when residents can't connect, when there's a security incident—who owns the problem? Vendors with multiple subcontractors, reseller relationships and fragmented support create finger-pointing scenarios where problems don't get solved. Elauwit Connection operates as one accountable partner: we design, build, monitor and support the network end-to-end. When something goes wrong, there's one phone number to call and one team that owns the fix. Accountability features to evaluate Single point of contact: Determine whether you'll deal with one organization or multiple vendors pointing at each other. Escalation authority: Understand who has the authority to make decisions when issues require immediate resolution. Track record: Ask for references from properties similar to yours and ask specifically about how problems were handled. Accountability question pros and cons Pros Cons Separates operators from resellers and aggregators Single-source providers may have limited geographic reach Predicts how problems will be handled before they occur Accountability claims require verification through references Reduces property team involvement in vendor coordination True accountability comes with corresponding expectations on both sides Comparison table: Key evaluation criteria for managed WiFi vendors Evaluation Criteria Elauwit Connection Typical Legacy ISP Regional MSP 24/7 Live Human Support ✓ Limited hours Varies Owner Network Ownership Option ✓ ✗ Varies $0 Upfront Capital Option ✓ ✗ Varies Single Accountable Partner ✓ ✗ ✓ What makes student housing WiFi requirements different from conventional multifamily? Student housing properties face connectivity challenges that conventional multifamily doesn't. Move-in happens in days rather than months. Device density runs higher because students bring laptops, tablets, gaming consoles and smart speakers. And residents are digital natives who notice network performance issues immediately. The network architecture needs to handle these realities. That means capacity for sudden surges, robust roaming across study areas and common spaces, and support that can scale during peak periods. Vendors with student housing experience understand these patterns. Those without it often underestimate what the network needs to deliver. Elauwit Connection has deployed managed WiFi across student housing communities and conventional multifamily properties for more than 20 years. That experience informs how we design networks for each property type's specific operational patterns. How does managed WiFi affect property value at sale? When you sell a property, the connectivity infrastructure matters. Buyers evaluate NOI, and managed WiFi that generates recurring revenue contributes to that number. They also assess operational complexity, and a network that runs without property team involvement is more attractive than one that creates ongoing management burden. The ownership structure matters at sale. Owner-owned infrastructure transfers as a property asset. Service-only arrangements may require contract assignment or renegotiation with the new owner. Understanding these implications before deployment helps you make decisions that align with your hold period and exit strategy. Industry data shows that properties with professional managed connectivity command premium valuations. The specific impact depends on your market, your property type and how well the network performs in practice. Why Elauwit Connection is a trusted managed WiFi partner for multifamily and student housing Elauwit Connection designs, builds and operates managed WiFi networks exclusively for residential communities. We're the only publicly traded managed service provider dedicated to multifamily and student housing, which means public accountability, disclosed performance and the financial stability that comes with it. With 38,000+ units under contract across 25 states and more than 20 years focused exclusively on residential properties, we understand what moves NOI versus what just looks good in a pitch deck. We answer resident support calls with real humans in less than 30 seconds. We offer flexible ownership structures that match your capital strategy. And we operate as one accountable partner from design through ongoing support. If you're evaluating managed WiFi providers for your multifamily or student housing property, contact Elauwit Connection to discuss how we can help you deliver premium connectivity while protecting your property economics. FAQs about managed WiFi for multifamily and student housing What is the typical deployment timeline for managed WiFi in an existing property? Deployment timelines typically range from 3-6 months depending on property size, existing infrastructure and construction coordination requirements. Elauwit Connection works with property teams to develop a structured deployment plan that minimizes disruption to current residents while meeting your operational deadlines. How does managed WiFi differ from bulk internet service? Bulk internet puts a residential gateway in each unit with residents managing their own WiFi. Managed WiFi is different. Elauwit Connection designs and operates the entire network, so residents get professional-grade connectivity without configuring equipment. Support comes directly from us, not from the resident troubleshooting their own router. Can managed WiFi generate revenue for property owners? Yes. Managed WiFi can create new recurring revenue through resident fees while reducing operational burden on property teams. Elauwit Connection offers revenue-share structures where properties earn from connectivity fees. The specific economics depend on your property, your market and the structure you choose. What happens if the managed WiFi service doesn't meet expectations? This is why contract terms and accountability structures matter. Ask vendors about service level commitments, escalation procedures and exit provisions before signing. Elauwit Connection operates as one accountable partner with clear performance expectations and transparent contract terms. Is managed WiFi required for smart building technology and IoT? A robust network foundation is essential for smart building systems, access control and IoT devices. Elauwit Connection designs networks that support these capabilities with appropriate segmentation for resident traffic, building systems, and guest access. body_text: BOTHELL, Wash. – Immunome, Inc. (the “Company”) (Nasdaq: IMNM), a biotechnology company focused on developing first-in-class and best-in-class targeted cancer therapies, announced today that on August 3, 2026, the Compensation Committee of the Company’s Board of Directors (the “Compensation Committee”) granted inducement awards consisting of non-statutory stock options to purchase an aggregate of 176,500 shares of common stock to nine new employees under the Company’s 2024 Inducement Plan. The stock options are subject to the terms and conditions of the Company’s 2024 Inducement Plan and the terms and conditions of an applicable stock option agreement covering the grant. About Immunome, Inc. Immunome is a clinical-stage targeted oncology company committed to developing first-in-class and best-in-class targeted cancer therapies. We are advancing an innovative portfolio of therapeutics, supported by a leadership team with deep experience in the design, development, and commercialization of cutting-edge therapies, including antibody-drug conjugates. Our pipeline includes varegacestat, an investigational gamma secretase inhibitor for which an NDA has been accepted by the U.S. FDA; IM-1021, a clinical-stage ROR1 ADC; IM-1617, a clinical-stage solid tumor ADC; and IM-3050, a clinical-stage FAP-targeted radiotherapy. body_text: Delcath Systems Reports Second Quarter 2026 Results and Business Highlights August 6, 2026 PDF Version Increases 2026 Revenue Guidance to a Range of $104M to $108M Conference Call Today at 8:30 a.m. Eastern Time QUEENSBURY, N.Y.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Aug. 6, 2026-- Delcath Systems, Inc. (Nasdaq: DCTH), an interventional oncology company focused on the treatment of primary and metastatic liver cancers, today announced financial results and business highlights for the second quarter ended June 30, 2026. Second Quarter 2026 Financial Results Total revenue of $29.1 million, compared with $24.2 million in the second quarter of 2025 HEPZATO KIT™ revenue of $27.1 million, compared to $22.5 million in the second quarter of 2025 CHEMOSAT® revenue of $2.0 million, compared to $1.7 million in the second quarter of 2025 Gross margins of 90%, compared to 86% in the second quarter of 2025 Net income of $2.7 million for both second quarters in 2026 and 2025 Non-GAAP adjusted EBITDA of $7.6 million, compared to $9.8 million in the second quarter of 2025 Cash provided by operations of $5.7 million in the quarter; compared to $7.3 million in the second quarter of 2025 Cash and investments of $95.9 million as of June 30, 2026 Business Highlights Currently 31 active treatment centers Approximately 30% growth in HEPZATO volume in the second quarter 2026 compared to the second quarter 2025 Independent investigators presented retrospective data at ESMO Breast Cancer 2026 showing a 60% hepatic partial response rate with percutaneous hepatic perfusion in heavily pretreated patients with liver-dominant metastatic breast cancer Independent investigators presented two investigator-initiated Trials-in-Progress abstracts at ASCO 2026: one evaluating sequential HEPZATO followed by tebentafusp in metastatic uveal melanoma, and one evaluating HEPZATO in combination with nivolumab/relatlimab in metastatic cutaneous melanoma with liver metastases Dosed the first patient in the global Phase 2 trial of HEPZATO in combination with standard of care in patients with liver-dominant HER2-negative metastatic breast cancer “Our strong second quarter, including total revenue of $29.1 million and quarterly operating cash flow of $5.7 million, reflects continued momentum in HEPZATO procedures,” said Gerard Michel, Chief Executive Officer of Delcath Systems. “As we grow our active treatment center network and drive physician adoption, we are seeing increased usage of HEPZATO in combination with systemic therapies to treat metastatic uveal melanoma. The growing clinical experience with this treatment strategy is strengthening physician confidence in HEPZATO and supporting its development as a multi-indication, liver-directed therapy platform, including colorectal and breast cancer.” 2026 Full Year Financial Guidance The Company’s financial outlook for fiscal year 2026: Total HEPZATO KIT and CHEMOSAT revenue to range from $104 million to $108 million, reflecting an increase in HEPZATO KIT volume of at least 28% over 2025 Full year gross margins in the range of 86% to 89% Positive adjusted EBITDA Second Quarter 2026 Results Total revenue for the quarter ending June 30, 2026 was $29.1 million compared to $24.2 million for the same period in the prior year. Revenue in the quarter includes sales of $27.1 million of HEPZATO in the U.S. and $2.0 million of CHEMOSAT in Europe. Research and development expenses for the quarter ending June 30, 2026, were $10.4 million compared to $6.9 million for the same period in the prior year. The increase is primarily due to increased clinical headcount and increased clinical trial activity. About Delcath Systems, Inc., HEPZATO KIT and CHEMOSAT Delcath Systems, Inc. is an interventional oncology company focused on the treatment of primary and metastatic liver cancers. The company's proprietary products, HEPZATO KIT™ (HEPZATO (melphalan) for Injection/Hepatic Delivery System) and CHEMOSAT® Hepatic Delivery System (HDS) for Melphalan percutaneous hepatic perfusion (PHP), are designed to administer high-dose chemotherapy to the liver while controlling systemic exposure and associated side effects during a PHP procedure. In the United States, HEPZATO KIT is considered a combination drug and device product and is regulated and approved for sale as a drug by the FDA. HEPZATO KIT is comprised of the chemotherapeutic drug melphalan and Delcath’s proprietary HDS. The HDS is used to isolate the hepatic venous blood from the systemic circulation while simultaneously filtrating hepatic venous blood during melphalan infusion and washout. The use of the HDS results in loco-regional delivery of a relatively high melphalan dose, which can potentially induce a clinically meaningful tumor response with minimal hepatotoxicity and reduce systemic exposure. HEPZATO KIT is approved in the United States as a liver-directed treatment for adult patients with metastatic uveal melanoma (mUM) with unresectable hepatic metastases affecting less than 50% of the liver and no extrahepatic disease, or extrahepatic disease limited to the bone, lymph nodes, subcutaneous tissues, or lung that is amenable to resection or radiation. Please see the full Prescribing Information, including BOXED WARNING for the HEPZATO KIT. In Europe, the device-only configuration of the HDS is regulated as a Class III medical device and is approved for sale under the trade name CHEMOSAT Hepatic Delivery System for Melphalan, or CHEMOSAT, where it has been used in the conduct of percutaneous hepatic perfusion procedures at major medical centers to treat a wide range of cancers of the liver. title: Artificial Fragrances in Skincare Products
summary: Artificial fragrances are commonly used in skincare and beauty products to give them a pleasant smell. But what are they, and why are they controversial?
body_text: Artificial fragrances are commonly used in skincare and beauty products to give them a pleasant smell. But what are they, and why are they controversial? Artificial fragrances are chemical compounds that are designed to mimic the scent of natural ingredients. They are typically made in a lab, and are used to give products a specific scent. They can be found in a wide range of products, including lotions, creams, perfumes, and makeup. While artificial fragrances can make a product smell nice, they can also be a source of concern for some people. One of the main concerns about artificial fragrances is that they can cause skin irritation and allergic reactions in some people. This is particularly true for people with sensitive skin, as the chemicals in artificial fragrances can be harsh. Another concern about artificial fragrances is that they can be a source of indoor air pollution. When products containing artificial fragrances are used, the chemicals can be released into the air, and can be inhaled. This can lead to respiratory problems, headaches, and other symptoms in some people. Many people choose to avoid products that contain artificial fragrances, especially those with sensitive skin. If you’re concerned about artificial fragrances in your skincare products, there are a few things you can do to avoid them. One way is to look for products that are labeled as “fragrance-free.” Many companies now offer fragrance-free alternatives to their products, which can provide peace of mind for those who are concerned about the safety of artificial fragrances. Another way to avoid artificial fragrances is to read the ingredient list on your skincare products. Artificial fragrances are typically listed as “fragrance” or “parfum” on the ingredient list. If you see any of these ingredients listed, it’s a good indication that the product contains artificial fragrances. In conclusion, artificial fragrances are commonly used in skincare and beauty products to give them a pleasant smell. They can cause skin irritation and allergic reactions in some people, and can be a source of indoor air pollution. If you’re concerned about artificial fragrances in your skincare products, look for products that are labeled as “fragrance-free” or check the ingredient list, and avoid products that contain them. Written by Clear, 24-01-2023

Its dashboards, summaries, and visualizations can help teams spot patterns and move faster, but business and lending decisions still belong to the people responsible for making them. title: Meta Launches New Open Models to Revive AI Strategy
summary: Meta unveils new open-source AI models as part of a strategic pivot to catch up with OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic in the competitive AI landscape.
body_text: Meta has officially launched a new generation of open-source AI models, marking another strategic pivot as the company struggles to keep pace with rivals like OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic. CEO Mark Zuckerberg announced the initiative as a fundamental shift in how Meta approaches artificial intelligence development, betting that openness will help the company regain ground in an increasingly competitive landscape. Release Date and Availability Officially released on August 2026, the new suite of open models represents Meta's most significant AI announcement this year. The models are available immediately through Meta's developer platforms, with full weights and training documentation accessible to researchers and enterprises. According to the company, this release schedule aims to establish Meta as the go-to provider for organizations seeking alternatives to closed, proprietary systems from competitors. Strategic Shift to Open Development Meta's renewed focus on open-source AI comes after months of trailing behind competitors in both consumer adoption and enterprise deployment. While ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini have captured mainstream attention, Meta's previous AI offerings struggled to gain similar traction. Zuckerberg's new strategy centers on three core principles: Full model weights released publicly, enabling customization and fine-tuning Transparent training methodologies and architecture documentation Commercial licensing that permits broad business use cases The approach directly challenges the closed-model strategies of OpenAI and Anthropic, positioning Meta as the champion of AI democratization. Industry observers note this mirrors Meta's historical playbook with React and PyTorch, where open-sourcing critical technologies helped establish industry standards while reducing Meta's own development costs. Technical Capabilities and Performance According to Meta's technical documentation, the new models demonstrate competitive performance across reasoning, coding, and multimodal tasks. Benchmark results shared by the company show improvements in mathematical problem-solving and extended context handling compared to Meta's previous releases. The models reportedly feature enhanced safety guardrails and reduced hallucination rates, addressing two critical concerns from earlier iterations. The release includes multiple model sizes, ranging from efficient edge-deployment versions to large-scale models requiring significant compute resources. This tiered approach allows developers to select appropriate models based on their specific latency, cost, and performance requirements. Competitive Landscape Challenges Meta faces substantial obstacles in executing this strategic reboot. OpenAI maintains strong enterprise relationships and brand recognition, while Google leverages deep integration across its product ecosystem. Anthropic has carved out a reputation for safety-focused AI, and specialized providers continue capturing niche markets. Meta's previous AI initiatives, including its conversational AI products and creator tools, have seen limited adoption outside the company's core social platforms. The timing of this release coincides with increasing regulatory scrutiny of AI development practices. Meta's open approach could either position the company favorably with policymakers advocating for transparency or invite criticism about releasing powerful capabilities without sufficient oversight. What This Means Meta's latest AI strategy represents a calculated gamble that openness will differentiate the company in a market dominated by proprietary systems. By making powerful models freely available, Meta aims to build a developer ecosystem that could eventually rival the commercial success of its competitors. Whether this approach succeeds depends on adoption rates, model performance in real-world applications, and Meta's ability to sustain investment in open development while competitors continue advancing closed systems. For enterprises evaluating AI providers, Meta's new models offer a credible alternative with full customization capabilities, though questions remain about long-term support and competitive performance as the technology evolves.

title: Verifying a Business with Claude: KYB and Beneficial Owners Through the Didit MCP
summary: Use Claude for KYB: create one parent session, follow configured Key People checks, review registry evidence, and keep final decisions human-owned.
body_text: Back to blog Blog · August 3, 2026 Verifying a Business with Claude: KYB and Beneficial Owners Through the Didit MCP Use Claude to create one parent KYB session, follow the hosted Key People flow, read registry and child KYC evidence, and keep policy decisions human-owned. From $2.00 per business. By Didit · August 3, 2026 · Updated Aug 3, 2026 Key takeaways In Claude, an operator creates one parent Know Your Business (KYB) session with a configured KYB workflow. Didit’s hosted flow—not Claude—automatically spawns child Know Your Customer (KYC) sessions according to the workflow’s Key People settings. KYC is not mandatory for every Ultimate Beneficial Owner (UBO). Ownership thresholds, required roles, and skip rules are configurable, and the applicable legal threshold depends on the jurisdiction and policy. didit_verify_kyb_search returns registry candidates. It does not traverse corporate relationships. A selected candidate can be resolved with didit_verify_kyb_select . Claude is useful as the conversational control surface: you ask it to create the parent session, explain returned states, summarize party progress, and assemble evidence. A human still selects the correct company and makes policy decisions. Didit Business Verification starts from $2.00 per business . Didit covers 220+ countries and territories, and each feature includes 500 free verifications per month. A business-verification conversation with Claude should feel simple without pretending the underlying compliance work is simple. The operator names the company and the approved workflow. Claude calls the relevant Didit tools. The business representative completes the hosted flow. Didit resolves registry and Key People requirements. Claude then turns the resulting records into a readable case summary. This article focuses on that conversation: what you type, what Claude should return, and what a human still decides. For the product mechanics, ownership data, and the broader Business Verification lifecycle, read KYB with the Didit MCP server . For Claude setup, use the connector installation guide . Before the conversation: configure the policy Claude should not invent your KYB policy. Configure a KYB workflow in Didit first. Its Key People settings determine which people connected to a business must complete child KYC sessions. Those settings can use ownership thresholds, require verification for specific roles such as directors or representatives, and skip KYC where your approved policy allows it. A 25% ownership threshold is common in some regulatory contexts, but it is not universal. Jurisdiction, customer type, risk level, control rights, and your organization’s obligations can change which people must be identified or verified. The workflow configuration expresses that policy; Claude executes against it. Connect through the Didit custom connector for Claude . The hosted endpoint uses OAuth (Open Authorization) 2.1 with PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange), so Claude acts with the signed-in user’s existing organization role. Conversation 1: confirm context and workflow Start by asking Claude to identify where it will operate. This matters when an analyst can access several organizations or applications: Call didit_context_get. State the selected Didit organization and application. Do not create or update anything. Then ask for the configured workflows: List my workflows and show only those configured for business verification. Return each name and workflow_id. For the workflow I choose, summarize its Key People requirements without changing them. Claude can use didit_workflow_list to show the available definitions. Read the summary carefully. If the workflow requires directors, representatives, or owners above a configured threshold, those are workflow rules—not recommendations generated by Claude. If the summary is ambiguous, stop and inspect the workflow in the Business Console before starting the business session. Conversation 2: optionally check the registry candidate For a pre-check, you can ask Claude to search an official registry: Search the United Kingdom registry for “Acme Trading Limited” using country_code GB. Return the candidate registered names, registration numbers, statuses, and kyb_response_id values. Do not select a candidate. Claude calls didit_verify_kyb_search . The response is a candidate list, not a verified ownership graph; the search tool does not traverse subsidiary or parent-company relationships. Similar names, former names, and reused trading names can produce several plausible candidates. The operator chooses the matching legal entity using evidence such as registration number, jurisdiction, and registered address. Then ask Claude to resolve that candidate: Select kyb_response_id KYB_CANDIDATE_ID and return the full registry record. Separate registry facts from any interpretation. Flag missing fields and do not infer owners that are absent. didit_verify_kyb_select resolves the chosen candidate. Claude can format the record and point out inconsistencies, but the human owns candidate selection. A fluent summary is not proof that the correct “Acme” was selected. Conversation 3: create one parent KYB session The hosted KYB flow begins with one session created from the selected KYB workflow: Create one business verification session using workflow_id 11111111-2222-3333-4444-555555555555. Set vendor_data to merchant-2048. Return the parent session_id and url only. Claude calls didit_session_create . The required argument is workflow_id ; the workflow defines that this is a KYB session. The response includes the parent session_id and hosted url . Send that URL to the authorized business representative through your approved channel. Claude must not call didit_session_create once per owner and claim those ad hoc sessions are linked to the business. That is not the KYB orchestration model. As the representative completes the hosted business flow, Didit automatically spawns the required child KYC sessions according to the parent workflow’s Key People settings. The configured rules determine which parties must verify; skip settings and per-role requirements remain effective. The end user sees the hosted business flow: requests for company information or documents required by the workflow, registry-resolution steps where applicable, and invitations or handoffs for the Key People who must complete KYC. The exact experience depends on configuration and available registry data. It is not a universal “verify every UBO” sequence. Conversation 4: read the parent state correctly Ask Claude to retrieve the actual parent decision rather than estimate completion time: Retrieve the decision for parent KYB session 66666666-7777-8888-9999-000000000000. Report the parent status, business findings, required Key People, and the completion state of each linked child KYC party. Do not infer missing parties or mark the business approved. Claude calls didit_session_get_decision and summarizes what Didit returned. The Awaiting User state has a specific KYB meaning: the parent business session is waiting while required child KYC parties finish. It is not a generic label for any missing business information. Do not attach the sub-2-second p99 inference figure to the overall KYB response time. A business flow can include human document collection, registry availability, and multiple people completing hosted child sessions. Claude should report current states, not promise a completion window. A useful follow-up prompt is: Turn this KYB decision into an analyst checklist with four sections: verified registry facts, completed Key People checks, unresolved or conflicting evidence, and decisions that require a human. Include record identifiers beside every finding. Conversation 5: screen and review without overclaiming If the workflow or policy calls for Anti-Money Laundering (AML) screening, ask Claude first whether a current result already exists. Avoid paying for a duplicate check merely because a new conversation started: Check the existing KYB decision for entity and Key People AML results. If a required current result is absent, show the exact subject data you would submit to didit_verify_aml and wait for approval before running a new screening. didit_verify_aml screens against 1,300+ sanctions, Politically Exposed Person (PEP), and adverse-media lists. Returned matches are candidates for analysis, not automatic proof that the business or person is prohibited. A human reviewer must resolve identity similarity, jurisdiction, dates, source reliability, and the organization’s escalation policy. What Claude returns, and what the human decides Claude can return: registry candidates, a selected registry record, the parent session link, current parent status, linked-party progress, screening results, and a source-labeled evidence summary. The human selects: the correct legal entity when candidates are ambiguous and the approved workflow before the session starts. The configured workflow determines: ownership thresholds, required roles, and allowed KYC skips for Key People. The human reviews: ownership or control ambiguity, registry gaps, potential AML matches, exceptions, and the final risk decision. The Business Console remains useful: when an analyst needs a visual ownership view, policy configuration, or a controlled review surface beyond the chat summary. Business Verification starts from $2.00 per business. A linked full KYC bundle, when required by the configured Key People rules, is $0.33 and includes ID verification, passive liveness, face match, and IP analysis. Each feature includes 500 free verifications per month. The MCP server itself is free. Resources Didit MCP GitHub repository — public source under the MIT license MCP overview — endpoint, transport, and connector model MCP tools documentation — canonical inputs and outputs Didit MCP developer page — product overview Didit MCP tools reference — conversational tool catalog The practical value is not an imaginary autonomous ownership investigation. It is a controlled conversation around a real KYB workflow: one parent session, automatically managed child KYC requirements, evidence returned from Didit, and a human decision at the points where law and risk policy require judgment.

title: Accounting Automation for High-Volume Businesses: How Finance Teams Scale
summary: Learn how accounting automation supports high-volume businesses with faster reconciliations, accurate books, AI-driven workflows and scalable finance operations.
body_text: When a business reaches a certain transaction velocity, the accounting engine that once worked begins to strain. High-volume environments generate a continuous stream of entries, card transactions, supplier invoices, refunds, reversals, bank movements, multi-platform sales, and VAT-linked documentation. What breaks first is not the accounting system; it’s the team’s capacity to keep pace with the volume while maintaining accuracy. Finance leaders across retail, logistics, e-commerce, hospitality, and multi-entity groups in the UAE report the same challenges: reconciliation cycles that stretch into late evenings, inconsistent coding across teams, fragmented documentation for VAT evidence, and month-end closes that slip unpredictably. Automation has moved from an efficiency preference to an operational necessity, not to reduce headcount, but to allow the finance team to operate with precision at scale. High-volume businesses don’t require more accountants; they require smarter, real-time workflows that eliminate repetitive tasks, reduce errors, and allow teams to focus on exception handling rather than rebuilding data. In this blog, we’ll explore why high-volume environments outgrow manual accounting, the areas where automation makes the greatest impact, and how finance teams can structure automation for scale. Key Takeaways High-volume businesses outgrow manual accounting fast; automation is essential for consistent coding, VAT compliance, and predictable month-end closes. Automation reduces errors by capturing data in real time and processing it with rules rather than manual judgment. Reconciliation, AP workflows, AR matching, VAT documentation, and multi-entity alignment benefit the most from automation. Finance teams must build automation on top of clean COA structures, integrated systems, and strong approval rules. Challenges High-Volume Finance Teams Face Without Automation Manual workflows do not deteriorate gradually; they fail suddenly once transaction volume crosses a threshold. Below are the pain points most UAE finance teams raise during audits or process reviews. Manual Data Entry and High Error Rates When thousands of entries flow through multiple channels each month, manual data entry inevitably introduces inconsistencies. Even a small error rate compounds into: Misposted expenses Incorrect VAT treatment Vendor disputes Adjustments during audits or CT filings The higher the volume, the less sustainable manual accuracy becomes. Slow Reconciliation Across Banks, Cards and Platforms Reconciling bank feeds, card statements, payment gateways, POS systems, and marketplace payouts manually creates backlogs that slow down cash-flow reporting. The more sources a business relies on, the longer reconciliation gaps become, eventually pushing month-end timelines beyond control. Unpredictable Month-End Close Cycles When reconciliations depend on spreadsheet patching, late invoices, or missing receipts, the close cycle becomes unpredictable. Leadership loses confidence in reporting timelines, and auditors face inconsistent records. Disjointed Systems and Spreadsheet Dependencies High-volume businesses often use multiple systems: ERP, e-commerce platforms, POS tools, supplier portals, and banking channels. When these do not communicate, finance must rebuild data manually in spreadsheets. This duplication limits scalability and increases the risk of discrepancies. VAT Compliance Gaps Due to Incomplete Documentation Missing TRNs, incorrect invoice formats, and unsupported transactions are common in volume-heavy environments. These gaps impact both VAT submissions and the accuracy of accounting books. Also read: Understanding Recording Business Expenses What Accounting Automation Means for High-Volume Environments Automation is not a piece of software; it is a shift in how accounting work is structured. For high-volume businesses, the objective is consistency, control, and predictable reporting. 1. Real-Time Data Capture From Multiple Sources Automated data capture ensures transactions from bank feeds, corporate cards, sales platforms, and vendor systems enter the accounting environment immediately. This prevents backlog accumulation and reduces dependency on end-of-month uploads. 2. Automated Categorisation and Coding Based on Rules High-volume teams benefit from rule-based classification: Vendor-specific coding Recurring transaction logic Tax category mapping Department-level routing This reduces manual decisions and standardises the accounting output. 3. Continuous Reconciliation Instead of Month-End Bulk Work Automation enables reconciliations to happen daily rather than monthly. Errors surface early, discrepancies are resolved faster, and the close cycle becomes structured rather than rushed. 4. Exception Handling Instead of Manual Checking Instead of scanning every transaction, teams only review items that fall outside rules, duplicates, mismatches, missing documents, or coding exceptions. This shifts their work from clerical review to control oversight. 5. AI Support for Document Extraction and Error Detection AI accelerates accuracy by extracting VAT details, supplier information, dates, and totals from receipts and invoices. In high-volume environments, this consistency is difficult to achieve manually. [cta-5] Also read: Modern Expense Management Guide Key Areas Where Automation Improves Accounting Performance High-volume businesses rarely struggle because they lack visibility; they struggle because the volume of operational tasks outpaces the team’s ability to process them consistently. Automation addresses the areas where scale creates the most friction. 1. Accounts Payable Workflows In high-volume environments, AP teams handle a mix of recurring invoices, one-off vendor bills, contract-based charges, and purchase-linked payables. Manual processes often result in: Late postings Duplicate entries Incorrect coding Misaligned VAT treatment Automation standardises invoice capture, extracts VAT-relevant fields instantly, and routes invoices through predefined approval rules. This reduces the time spent verifying documentation and correcting coding errors. 2. Accounts Receivable and Cash Application Businesses with high sales volumes often struggle with matching incoming payments to invoices or platform payouts. Automation helps: Match receipts to open invoices Identify short payments or discrepancies Update ageing schedules in real time This gives finance leaders clearer visibility into cash flow and reduces the manual workload tied to collections. 3. Bank and Card Reconciliation For high-volume companies, daily reconciliation is impossible without automation. Automated matching compares: Bank statement lines Card transactions Platform payouts ERP ledger entries It identifies discrepancies instantly, reducing end-of-month bottlenecks and improving reporting accuracy. 4. VAT Documentation and Filing Accuracy VAT compliance becomes increasingly difficult as transaction volume grows. Automation helps by: Capturing all receipts and invoices at the point of spend Extracting VAT amounts and TRN details Ensuring invoices meet UAE VAT requirements Reducing exposure to input VAT disallowances This improves both monthly VAT returns and year-end accounting accuracy. 5. Multi-Entity and Multi-Location Accounting Groups operating across multiple entities or branches often face: Different coding practices Inconsistent COA structures Manual intercompany entries Automation enforces standardisation and ensures all entities follow the same rules across coding, categorisation and document capture. Also read: ERP Integration Benefits Explained How High-Volume Businesses Should Structure Their Automation Workflow Automation cannot succeed without a reliable system foundation. For high-volume teams, the workflow must be built on consistency and data discipline, not just software adoption. Standardising the Chart of Accounts to Support Automation A unified chart of accounts ensures that automation rules behave predictably across the organisation. It prevents overlapping categories, duplicate expense types, and ambiguous coding logic that introduce inconsistencies at scale. When each category is clearly defined and applied uniformly across departments and locations, automation can classify transactions accurately without repeated intervention from finance. Defining Rules for Coding, Categorisation and Approvals Rule-based logic gives high-volume teams predictable workflows. These rules can reflect vendor type, cost centre, spend category, VAT applicability, or recurring transaction patterns. By structuring logic around how the organisation actually spends, finance reduces manual judgment calls and ensures that expense coding remains consistent, even as volume increases. This reduces rework at month-end and supports cleaner financial reporting. Integrating ERP, Expense Management and Banking Systems Automation only works when systems communicate. High-volume businesses should ensure: ERP integrations run continuously Banking feeds update automatically Expense management tools sync transactions in real time This eliminates data silos and gives finance teams a single source of truth. Maintaining Data Quality for Reliable Automated Processing Automation amplifies both good and bad data. If inputs are inconsistent, incorrect vendor names, missing documents, or wrong tax mapping, errors multiply at scale. Clean data governance is essential. Redesigning Roles Around Review, Analysis and Controls As automation takes over repetitive processing tasks, finance teams shift towards work that strengthens oversight and decision-making. This includes managing exceptions, analysing variances, enforcing spend policies, and monitoring internal controls. Redesigning roles toward review and analysis ensures that automation enhances, not replaces, the team’s impact. The result is a finance function that operates with greater efficiency and a clearer focus on risk, accuracy, and strategic insight. Also read: Understanding Chart of Accounts Indicators That a Business Is Ready for Accounting Automation Most high-volume companies don’t realise they’ve crossed the automation threshold until operational strain becomes visible. These signals are common across UAE SMEs and mid-market businesses. 1. Frequent Backlogs in Reconciliation and Invoice Processing If reconciliations regularly fall behind schedule, volume has exceeded team capacity. 2. Increasing Volume Outgrowing Team Capacity When hiring more accountants becomes the only short-term solution, automation provides a more scalable long-term answer. 3. High Dependence on Spreadsheets to Patch Data If Excel becomes the place where data is “fixed,” the underlying systems are not supporting the volume. 4. Repeated VAT Adjustments or Documentation Gaps Missing invoices, incorrect VAT mapping, and inconsistent recovery claims are signs that manual processes are no longer reliable. 5. Unpredictable Close Cycles Impacting Reporting Performance instability during month-end typically signals that processes need automation, not more effort. Also read: ERP Integration Challenges and Solutions How Alaan Supports Accounting Automation for High-Volume Companies Alaan helps finance teams reduce manual workload and improve accounting accuracy by ensuring that every stage of the spend-to-book process is automated, structured, and audit-ready. Real-Time Transaction Sync into ERPs At Alaan, we push transactions directly into ERPs such as Xero, QuickBooks, NetSuite, and Microsoft Dynamics. This removes the lag between when a payment happens and when it shows up in accounting. High-volume teams gain faster visibility over expenses and fewer surprises during reconciliation. ‍ Automated Receipt and Invoice Capture With VAT Checks Receipts and invoices are captured the moment a transaction occurs. Alaan Intelligence extracts supplier information, VAT amounts, TRN details, dates, and totals, and flags incomplete or non-compliant documentation. This ensures UAE VAT accuracy and reduces missing evidence issues at month-end. ‍ Cleaner Coding Through Policy-Based Controls Finance teams can define controls around spend categories, vendor types, department limits, and tax applicability. These rules prevent inaccurate entries from entering the system, reduce manual recoding later, and maintain consistent chart-of-accounts mapping. ‍ Faster Reconciliation With Complete Transaction Data Because every transaction contains correct coding, documentation, and policy validation upfront, reconciliation becomes a verification step rather than a clean-up exercise. High-volume businesses benefit from fewer exceptions and more predictable close cycles. ‍ Audit-Ready Records for Every Expense Each expense processed through Alaan contains a complete trail of who spent, what was purchased, receipt evidence, VAT extraction, coding, and approvals. This reduces the time spent preparing for audits and supports cleaner reviews across internal and external stakeholders. [cta-10] Also read: Post Expenses and VAT in ERP Systems Conclusion For high-volume businesses, automation is not just a way to streamline accounting; it is how finance maintains accuracy, compliance, and operational predictability as transaction volume grows. When data flows into the ERP in real time, coding follows consistent rules, VAT documentation is complete, and reconciliations run continuously, the finance function becomes significantly more scalable. Accounting automation gives finance leaders the confidence that the numbers are accurate, the close cycle is stable, and the organisation can support higher transaction volumes without adding complexity or unnecessary manual workload. At Alaan , we help high-volume businesses automate expense capture, VAT checks, ERP syncing, and reconciliation so your finance team can operate with accuracy at scale. If you want a clearer, more automated accounting workflow tailored to UAE requirements, you can book a demo and see how Alaan supports your current ERP and process structure. Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) 1. What does accounting automation mean for high-volume businesses? It refers to replacing manual data entry, coding, document capture, and reconciliation with automated workflows that process transactions in real time. This improves accuracy and reduces the time required to close books. 2. Which accounting tasks benefit most from automation? Accounts payable, accounts receivable matching, bank and card reconciliation, VAT documentation, and intercompany processing are the areas that typically see the greatest improvement. 3. How does automation impact month-end close timelines? By reconciling continuously and reducing manual corrections, automation makes the close cycle faster and more predictable. High-volume businesses often report significant reductions in close time. 4. Does automation replace accountants? No. It shifts their focus from data entry and corrections toward analysis, control, and exception handling. Automation supports the finance team; it doesn’t replace it. 5. Why is VAT evidence difficult to manage at high volumes? Large numbers of transactions increase the chances of missing invoices, incomplete documentation, or incorrect VAT mapping. Automated receipt capture and VAT extraction help maintain compliant records. 6. How does Alaan support accounting automation? Alaan syncs transactions into ERPs in real time, extracts VAT details from receipts, enforces coding and policy rules, and creates audit-ready records. This reduces reconciliation effort and improves accounting accuracy.

title: Chaos by Design: Why We Need to Break AI Network Fabrics on Purpose
summary: See how VIAVI is helping validate next-generation AI fabrics with UET and workload emulation.
body_text: Chaos by Design: Why We Need to Break AI Network Fabrics on Purpose Neil Holmquist August 7, 2026 Like Notes from the front lines of AI fabric validation, just in time for OCP APAC Summit 2026 Here’s an uncomfortable truth about AI networking: the failures that determine whether a fabric is production-ready rarely appear under normal operating conditions. Training clusters run for months. Collective operations complete successfully. Congestion clears and dashboards stay green. Everything appears healthy…until it doesn’t. A burst storm arrives at exactly the wrong moment or a credit pool depletes under an untested traffic pattern. Suddenly, the fabric that spent a year in qualification collapses in production, often when it matters most. The real issue isn’t that these failures occur. It’s that they’re entirely predictable. Traditional validation methods simply don’t recreate the conditions that expose them in a repeatable, measurable way. The Open AI Networking Ecosystem Has Arrived For years, open AI networking was more roadmap discussion than deployment reality. That changed quickly. UEC Specification 1.0 debuted in 2025. ESUN 1.0 released in March 2026. Broadcom introduced Tomahawk Ultra silicon engineered for scale-up Ethernet and demonstrated UEC LLR/CBFC interoperability at OFC 2026. Synopsys is licensing ESUN IP, and VIAVI showcased Ultra Ethernet Transport (UET) interoperability with HPE Juniper at Interop Tokyo 2025. This is no longer a discussion about future standards. Open AI networking is shipping today and increasingly finding its way into customer deployments. As a result, the industry’s fundamental question has shifted. The question is no longer “What should AI fabrics do?” but “How do we prove they will continue to do it under real-world conditions, failures, and scale?” Five Ways a “Healthy” Fabric Can Fail Across AI infrastructure deployments, the same classes of failures continue to surface. Burst storms: synchronized All-Reduce operations can overwhelm the fabric instantaneously in ways that everyday traffic rarely reproduces. Credit starvation: a large flow consumes available CBFC credits, starving other traffic sharing the same resources. Asymmetric load: uneven ECMP hashing concentrates traffic on certain paths while leaving others underutilized. Retry cascades: a single packet drop triggers retries, which generate additional congestion, causing further packet loss and even more retries. Head-of-line blocking: large flows occupy critical resources, delaying smaller latency-sensitive traffic and degrading overall application responsiveness. None of these scenarios are unusual. All occur in production environments. What’s concerning is that most traditional lab qualification testing rarely exposes them consistently enough to diagnose and fix the underlying issues. Inference Traffic Raises the Stakes If training traffic is challenging to validate, inference traffic is even more demanding. Modern LLM inference introduces a mix of traffic patterns that place unique stress on the network. Prefill and decode phases exchange state through KV-cache transfers that can range from hundreds of megabytes to tens of gigabytes. These large “elephant” transfers share infrastructure with latency-sensitive “mice” flows responsible for delivering tokens every few milliseconds. When a KV-cache transfer consumes credits at the wrong moment, decode traffic suffers and inter-token latency increases. User experience degrades. p99.9 service-level objectives are missed. This is not a theoretical edge case. It is a validation challenge that must be tested intentionally. The impact becomes even more pronounced at scale. A tail-latency event that appears insignificant at small GPU counts becomes almost inevitable in large clusters. At 64 GPUs, a 0.1% per-GPU tail-latency rate may appear occasionally. At 1,024 GPUs, that same rate becomes an expected occurrence at virtually every step. As infrastructures scale, worst-case behavior becomes normal behavior. Why NCCL Benchmarks Aren’t Enough Many organizations still rely heavily on NCCL-based benchmarks to validate AI fabrics. NCCL testing certainly provides useful data, but it has important limitations. Because NCCL generates self-regulated traffic patterns, engineers cannot independently control burst characteristics, arrival timing, flow size distributions, incast conditions, and cross-flow interactions. More importantly, NCCL benchmarks largely focus on application-level outcomes rather than fabric-level behavior. They measure throughput, but do not provide deep visibility into: Switch buffer occupancy Credit consumption and allocation Congestion development Flow interactions Tail-latency root causes Yet these are precisely the areas where fabric failures originate. Today, the AI networking ecosystem still lacks widely accepted validation standards, including common acceptance test suites, standardized chaos scenarios, agreed p99.9 performance thresholds, and consistent qualification criteria. As a result, every vendor is effectively defining “qualified” independently. Closing the Validation Gap with Workload Emulation This is where synthetic workload emulation becomes critical. Rather than waiting for production traffic to uncover weaknesses, engineers can intentionally create the conditions most likely to expose them. VIAVI TestCenter was built to enable exactly this approach, generating realistic AI workload traffic patterns deterministically, repeatably, and at line rate without requiring a live GPU cluster. With VIAVI TestCenter, teams can: Recreate burst storms, credit starvation, asymmetric ECMP load, retry cascades, and head-of-line blocking on demand Emulate KV-cache elephant-and-mice traffic interactions across varying context lengths and precision formats Measure p99.9 and tail-latency performance with visibility into switch buffers and credit behavior Compare firmware releases and hardware generations using identical, repeatable validation scenarios Validate multi-vendor interoperability before deployment by testing switches, NICs, and operating systems under controlled stress conditions Because these workloads are synthetic, the methodology remains protocol-agnostic. The same approach can be applied across RoCEv2/DCQCN and emerging UEC/ UET /CBFC environments, enabling meaningful comparisons. The value is not simply generating stress. It is generating stress that can be repeated, measured, and trusted. Moving from Reactive to Intentional Validation Open AI networking specifications have given the industry a blueprint for what AI fabrics should do. What remains missing is a shared, repeatable method for validating whether they continue to perform under the conditions that matter most. Workload emulation helps close that gap. As ESUN and UEC deployments continue to accelerate, now is the time for the industry to align on repeatable validation methodologies rather than learning these lessons through production incidents. Don’t wait for chaos to find your fabric. Instead, create it deliberately and test against it, measure it, and fix it. This is what we call “Chaos by Design.” See Chaos by Design in Action See how VIAVI is helping validate next-generation AI fabrics with UET and workload emulation. Watch our video to see UET performance and interoperability in action. In addition, join VIAVI at OCP APAC Summit 2026 “Chaos by Design” session to learn how workload emulation helps expose hidden AI fabric failure modes before deployment. title: Dia do Soldado: como explicar a data para crianças de forma simples e educativa
summary: Entenda por que o Dia do Soldado é celebrado em 25 de agosto e veja como explicar a data às crianças com atividades sobre história e cidadania.
body_text: Para as crianças, não é necessário apresentar todos os conflitos militares dos quais ele participou. A explicação pode se concentrar no fato de que se trata de um personagem da história do Brasil , deixando análises mais aprofundadas para estudantes maiores. Como explicar o Dia do Soldado para crianças? Uma explicação simples pode dizer que soldados são profissionais treinados para atuar na defesa do país e que, em determinadas situações, também podem participar de ações de apoio à população. A conversa pode começar com uma frase como: “O Dia do Soldado é lembrado em 25 de agosto. A data foi escolhida por ser o aniversário de Duque de Caxias, uma figura importante da história do Exército Brasileiro.” Depois da contextualização, o adulto pode perguntar o que a criança entende por cuidar de uma comunidade . Assim, a data abre espaço para conversar sobre responsabilidade, cooperação, respeito às regras e proteção das pessoas. Também é importante explicar que cidadania não depende de uma profissão específica. Professores, profissionais da saúde, bombeiros, agentes da Defesa Civil e moradores também colaboram para o bem-estar coletivo de diferentes maneiras. Como adaptar a explicação para cada idade? O conteúdo deve acompanhar o desenvolvimento da criança. Quanto menor a faixa etária, mais concreta, breve e lúdica precisa ser a abordagem. Etapa escolar Abordagem recomendada Conceitos que podem ser trabalhados Educação Infantil História curta, desenhos, músicas e brincadeiras cooperativas ajuda, cuidado, respeito e trabalho em equipe Anos iniciais do Ensino Fundamental Linha do tempo simples e conversa sobre profissões que protegem a população cidadania, responsabilidade, comunidade e símbolos nacionais Anos finais do Ensino Fundamental Pesquisa orientada e comparação entre fontes históricas contexto histórico, instituições públicas e pensamento crítico Ensino Médio Debate sobre o papel das Forças Armadas e a construção da memória histórica Estado, cidadania, direitos, deveres e análise de fontes Como abordar o Dia do Soldado na Educação Infantil? No Dia do Soldado na Educação Infantil , o foco pode permanecer nas experiências conhecidas pelas crianças. Compartilhar materiais, cumprir combinados, ajudar colegas e cuidar dos espaços coletivos são exemplos próximos da rotina. A brincadeira e a expressão artística tendem a ser mais adequadas do que longas explicações. A Revista Quero Bolsa também apresenta conteúdos sobre a importância do brincar para o desenvolvimento infantil . Não é necessário vestir as crianças com uniformes militares ou reproduzir marchas e combates. A data pode ser trabalhada como uma oportunidade de conhecer a história e valorizar atitudes de cooperação. Como conversar com crianças maiores? Crianças maiores já conseguem compreender que personagens históricos viveram em contextos diferentes e podem ser estudados sob mais de uma perspectiva. Uma pesquisa orientada sobre Duque de Caxias pode incluir perguntas como: Em que período da história brasileira ele viveu? Por que se tornou patrono do Exército? Quem escolhe quais personagens recebem homenagens? Como documentos e fontes diferentes apresentam a mesma pessoa? De que maneira as instituições públicas atuam atualmente? Esse tipo de atividade evita uma narrativa baseada apenas na memorização de nomes e datas. Também estimula a leitura, a argumentação e a análise crítica. Veja também: Avaliação de escola: como usar opiniões de pais para escolher onde matricular os filhos Quais atividades do Dia do Soldado podem ser feitas com crianças? As atividades do Dia do Soldado podem combinar história, arte, leitura e cidadania. O objetivo deve ser promover aprendizagem, sem incentivar violência ou rivalidade. Atividade Como realizar Aprendizagem estimulada Roda de conversa sobre cidadania As crianças apresentam exemplos de atitudes que ajudam a comunidade escuta, empatia e participação Linha do tempo ilustrada A turma organiza a data de nascimento de Duque de Caxias e outros acontecimentos estudados noção de tempo e pesquisa histórica Mural “Quem cuida da comunidade?” São reunidos desenhos de diferentes profissionais e cidadãos valorização do trabalho coletivo Missão de cooperação Pequenos grupos resolvem um desafio, como organizar livros ou montar um quebra-cabeça planejamento e trabalho em equipe Cartões de agradecimento As crianças escrevem para profissionais que ajudam a população escrita, reconhecimento e respeito Comparação de fontes Estudantes maiores consultam textos diferentes sobre a origem da data leitura crítica e verificação de informações Como fazer uma missão de cooperação? A turma pode receber uma tarefa que só seja concluída com a participação de todos. Organizar materiais, montar uma construção ou criar um mapa coletivo são algumas possibilidades. Ao final, o educador pode perguntar quais atitudes ajudaram o grupo. Escutar, dividir tarefas, respeitar o tempo dos colegas e buscar soluções em conjunto devem ser valorizados mais do que a velocidade. Como criar um mural sobre quem ajuda a comunidade? Cada criança pode escolher uma pessoa ou profissão que contribua para a sociedade. O mural pode reunir soldados, professores, profissionais da saúde, bombeiros, garis, familiares e voluntários. A proposta ajuda a mostrar que o cuidado com a coletividade possui muitas formas. Também favorece uma abordagem mais ampla de educação para a cidadania , tema que pode ser desenvolvido ao longo de todo o ano letivo. A relação entre cidadania, ética e cotidiano escolar é aprofundada no conteúdo sobre o Programa Educação para a Cidadania e Sustentabilidade . O que deve ser evitado ao trabalhar a data? A abordagem educativa deve evitar atividades que associem a figura do soldado exclusivamente a armas, batalhas ou força física. Entre os principais cuidados estão: não utilizar armas de brinquedo como recurso pedagógico; não apresentar conflitos como brincadeiras sem consequências; não obrigar crianças a vestir fantasias ou participar de encenações; não reforçar a ideia de que coragem significa ausência de medo; não limitar comportamentos ou profissões de acordo com o gênero; não apresentar personagens históricos como figuras sem contradições; não transformar a atividade em competição entre crianças. Caso surjam perguntas sobre guerras, a resposta deve ser verdadeira, curta e adequada à idade. Pode-se explicar que conflitos causam sofrimento e que diálogo, diplomacia e cooperação são caminhos importantes para a convivência entre povos. Como a família pode conversar sobre o tema em casa? A família pode começar perguntando o que foi aprendido na escola. Essa escuta permite identificar dúvidas, interpretações equivocadas ou assuntos que despertaram curiosidade. Livros, mapas, fotografias históricas e materiais de instituições confiáveis podem complementar a conversa. Para crianças menores, desenhos e jogos cooperativas costumam tornar o conteúdo mais compreensível. Também vale relacionar a data a atitudes cotidianas. Respeitar outras pessoas, cuidar dos espaços comuns, cumprir combinados e participar da comunidade são formas concretas de exercer cidadania. Perguntas frequentes sobre o Dia do Soldado Quando é comemorado o Dia do Soldado? O Dia do Soldado é comemorado em 25 de agosto no Brasil. A data corresponde ao nascimento de Duque de Caxias, patrono do Exército Brasileiro. Quem foi Duque de Caxias? Duque de Caxias foi o título recebido por Luís Alves de Lima e Silva, militar e político brasileiro do século XIX. Sua trajetória está ligada ao período imperial e a diferentes conflitos da história do país. Qual é o objetivo de trabalhar o Dia do Soldado na escola? A data pode ser usada para apresentar um tema da história brasileira e desenvolver reflexões sobre cidadania, responsabilidade, cooperação e atuação das instituições públicas. Crianças precisam se fantasiar de soldados? Não. Fantasias não são necessárias para compreender a data. Rodas de conversa, desenhos, pesquisas e desafios cooperativos oferecem possibilidades mais amplas de aprendizagem. O Dia do Soldado é feriado? Não. O dia 25 de agosto é uma data comemorativa, mas não é feriado nacional. Como tornar o Dia do Soldado uma experiência educativa? O Dia do Soldado pode ir além de uma homenagem isolada. Quando apresentado de maneira contextualizada, o tema contribui para que crianças conheçam a história, façam perguntas e compreendam que viver em sociedade envolve direitos, deveres, respeito e cooperação. Família e escola podem construir essa reflexão juntas, sempre considerando a idade dos estudantes e abrindo espaço para diferentes pontos de vista. A escolha de uma instituição com proposta pedagógica acolhedora também faz diferença nesse processo. Na Quero Bolsa, responsáveis podem pesquisar escolas e conhecer oportunidades de bolsas para a Educação Infantil, o Ensino Fundamental e o Ensino Médio . A Quero Escola é uma plataforma que conecta famílias a escolas particulares de todo o Brasil , oferecendo bolsas de estudo para Educação Infantil, Ensino Fundamental e Ensino Médio com descontos de até 80% .
