title: Electrical & Security Distribution: Scale Isn't the Digital Shelf
summary: Six of 40 electrical, data, and security distributors now hold a measured DRI; Grainger leads at 66, while the group's biggest name, Wesco, scores lowest at 40.
body_text: Part of Top Distributors 2026 — the Anglera Index: North America’s largest distributors ranked, classified into six operating archetypes, and scored on the measured Digital Readiness Index . Of the 40 electrical, data, and security distributors in this cut, only six had a public catalog we could actually measure for the Digital Readiness Index. That's not a comment on how big or well-run the other 34 are; several are among the largest companies in the vertical by revenue. It's a comment on how this channel builds its digital shelf. Wesco International , the largest company in the group at $23.5B (FY2025), has a corporate site that turned out to be brochureware with no scorable catalog attached; its real customer-facing storefront lives on a separate portal that blocks standard clients, so we measured it in a full browser session — disclosed on its scorecard — and it scored 40, the lowest mark in the cut. Rexel North America first came back with server errors, but an adversarial re-check found a live public catalog after all; it's verified live and not yet sampled, so it carries no score this edition. Among the six distributors we could actually score, W.W. Grainger leads at 66 out of 100 on the Digital Readiness Index , and even its page is a study in contrast between attribute richness and machine-matchable identifiers. The ranking Rank Company Revenue (FY) Archetype DRI 15 Wesco International $23.5B Scale-aggregator 40 19 Sonepar (North America) $19.0B (NA) Scale-aggregator 62 20 W.W. Grainger $17.9B Scale-aggregator 66 25 Graybar $12.9B Scale-aggregator 51 27 Rexel (North America) $10.1B (NA) Scale-aggregator not yet measured (catalog verified live) 31 Motion (Genuine Parts Company) ~$9.0B (segment) Branch-density 62 32 Winsupply $8.4B Branch-density not measured (no public catalog) 35 Fastenal $8.2B Program-supplier 55 51 Consolidated Electrical Distributors (CED) ~$5.5B (est.) Branch-density not yet measured (catalog verified live) 54 ADI Global Distribution $4.78B (segment) Catalog-native not in this sample 62 Border States $4.0B+ (est.) Scale-aggregator not in this sample 76 McNaughton-McKay Group $2.2B (dated) Technical-specialist not in this sample 78 Elliott Electric Supply $2.12B Branch-density not in this sample 84 Lonestar Electric Supply $1.7B Program-supplier not in this sample 92 RS Group (Americas) ~$1.09B (NA) Catalog-native not in this sample 93 Main Electric Supply Co. just under $1.1B Branch-density not in this sample 98 Van Meter Inc. $928.5M (dated) Branch-density not in this sample 99 Gresco Utility Supply $846M Technical-specialist not in this sample 105 Turtle $572M (est.) Technical-specialist not in this sample 111 IEWC $500M+ (est.) Technical-specialist not in this sample 116 Inline Electric Supply $456M Branch-density not in this sample 118 Rural Electric Supply Cooperative (RESCO) $404M Program-supplier / branch-density not sampled 122 Granite City Electric Supply $335M Branch-density not in this sample 124 United Electric Supply $300M+ (dated) Branch-density not in this sample — City Electric Supply not disclosed Branch-density not in this sample — Colonial Electric Supply not disclosed Branch-density not in this sample — Crescent Electric Supply Company not disclosed Branch-density not in this sample — Dealers Electrical Supply Company not disclosed Branch-density not in this sample — Green Mountain Electric Supply not disclosed PE-rollup not in this sample — Kendall Electric not disclosed Branch-density not in this sample — Kirby Risk not disclosed Technical-specialist not in this sample — Scott Electric not disclosed Branch-density not in this sample — State Electric Supply Company not disclosed Branch-density not in this sample — U.S. Electrical Services not disclosed Branch-density not in this sample — Werner Electric Supply not disclosed Technical-specialist not in this sample — Wholesale Electric Supply not disclosed Branch-density not in this sample — Wholesale Electrical Supply Co. of Houston not disclosed Program-supplier not in this sample — Dakota Supply Group (DSG) not disclosed Branch-density not sampled — Eckart Supply not disclosed Branch-density not sampled — Franklin Empire not disclosed Branch-density / technical-specialist not sampled Stacked bars: the four pillars of the Digital Readiness Index — segment lengths are pillar scores, the number is the company's total out of 100. Full index: Top Distributors 2026 . Branch density carries the field; scale sits on top of it Count primary archetypes across the 40 companies and branch-density wins by a wide margin: 21 of 40, more than half the vertical. Scale-aggregator and technical-specialist tie for a distant second at six apiece, with program-suppliers, catalog-native operators, and a single PE-rollup filling out the rest. That split maps cleanly onto how the channel actually sells. This is a trade-counter business built on contractor relationships and local stock, and the model shows up at every size, not just among the small independents. Winsupply does $8.4B (FY2026) through more than 680 "Local Companies," each with real local equity and P&L ownership held by its branch president rather than a national brand. Consolidated Electrical Distributors (CED) , at an estimated ~$5.5B, runs over 700 independently managed "profit centers" with branch-level pricing and purchasing autonomy; its old ced.com domain now redirects to an unrelated company, and the actual business lives across hundreds of separately branded local sites instead. The scale-aggregators sit at the top of the revenue list precisely because they've built the opposite of that: centralized buying power and, increasingly, a unified digital layer over an acquired branch footprint. Sonepar is the clearest case: the world's number-one B2B electrical distributor by its own account, it posted record global sales of $37.9B in 2025 and grew digital sales 50% to $13.9B through its Spark omnichannel platform, even while its 14 U.S. operating-company banners (Capital Electric, Codale, Irby, and others) keep running locally under their own names. Graybar is doing something similar from the infrastructure side: it finished a SAP S/4HANA overhaul in 2025, opened three new STAR distribution centers built for large data-center and construction accounts, and kept up its acquisition pace with roughly its 20th deal in a decade. Wesco's fastest-growing line is data centers too, at $4.3B in 2025 sales, up about 50% year over year. And Border States , at $4.0B+, made the opposite kind of move: it left the Affiliated Distributors buying group in December 2025 after 40 years, a step only a company with its own national-account-scale purchasing volume can take on its own. What the Digital Readiness Index found The six distributors we could measure split into distinct profiles rather than a tight cluster, and the pillar breakdown explains why more than the headline score does. The vertical's median DRI among measured companies is 62, running four points above the index-wide median of 58. Grainger's 66 is built on the deepest catalog in the group: a median of 47 structured attributes per sampled page, easily the richest of the six, and a product-data pillar score of 31 out of 35. But its GTIN rate on those same pages is 0%, meaning none of the sampled products carried a standard identifier a system elsewhere could use to confirm it's looking at the same item. Grainger also explicitly blocks AI crawlers, an active choice that cost it points on agent readiness (9 of 20) rather than a case of simply not having addressed the question. Sonepar's 62 comes from almost the opposite shape: a perfect agent-readiness score (20 of 20) and an 80% GTIN rate, but a median of just 9 attributes per page, tied with Wesco for the thinnest catalog of the six. Pricing is fully gated (0% public), consistent with a business selling through independently run regional banners to contractor accounts on quote. Motion , the Genuine Parts Company industrial arm, also scored 62, anchored by a perfect 20-of-20 transparency pillar, full public pricing, and no login wall on any product page. But it also posted the widest consistency spread in the sample, a 45-point gap between its richest and thinnest sampled category, the most uneven treatment of its own catalog among the six measured companies. Fastenal scored 55, the group's best answerability pillar (16.6 of 25) undercut by the thinnest product-data score (16.7 of 35) and no working sitemap, which dragged its agent readiness down to 6 of 20, tied with Wesco for the lowest of the six. Graybar's 51 reflects gated pricing, an explicit AI-crawler block, and the group's widest spread outside Motion (15 points), even though its product pages themselves are publicly browsable without an account. Wesco's 40 rounds out the group at the bottom: a respectable product-data pillar (21.1 of 35) on the pages a logged-out buyer sees, but a median of just 9 attributes, gated pricing, and an agent-readiness score built from what a standard client sees — which, on buy.wesco.com, is an HTTP 403. For a buyer of this vertical's products, the attribute gap is the whole ballgame. Specifying a breaker means filtering on voltage and amperage rating and trip curve; specifying cable means wire gauge, conduit trade size, and plenum-versus-riser jacket rating; specifying an enclosure or a security camera means NEMA/IP rating, UL or ETL listing, or lens type and resolution. A median of 9 attributes, Sonepar's number, likely covers brand, model, and category, not enough to answer any of those questions without a call to a counter rep. A median of 47, Grainger's number, can support that kind of filtering directly on the page. The missing identifier is the catch: even a fully specified page can't be confidently matched to the same SKU in a buyer's own item master , or in a competitor's catalog, without one. Where this is heading The biggest names in this vertical are pulling in a direction the branch-density majority hasn't followed yet: Sonepar's Spark platform, Wesco and Graybar's data-center buildouts, and ADI Global Distribution 's August 2026 spinoff from Resideo into a freestanding, NYSE-listed company all point toward treating a unified digital layer as core infrastructure rather than a website bolted onto branch operations. Border States leaving its buying group after 40 years to deal directly with vendors is a scale move in the same spirit. Underneath all of that, the majority of this vertical by company count is still running the branch-density model this measurement was never built to score at scale, and some of them are starting to close the gap through shared platforms rather than building their own: Granite City Electric Supply went live on Affiliated Distributors' eContent product-data platform on its webstore in mid-2026. That's likely the more common path for the long tail here than any of them building a national storefront from scratch.

title: What to Know About the New Pied-à-Terre Tax
summary: One of the campaign promises from Zohran Mamdani when he was running for Mayor in 2025 was that the rich would pay their fair share. On July 23rd, the first step towards fulfilling this measure was put into place. Property owners who may be subject to the “pied-à-terre”, or in layman’s terms “Second Home” tax […] The post What to Know About the New Pied-à-Terre Tax appeared first on Real Estate Topics, Tips, and Guides .
body_text: One of the campaign promises from Zohran Mamdani when he was running for Mayor in 2025 was that the rich would pay their fair share. On July 23rd, the first step towards fulfilling this measure was put into place. Property owners who may be subject to the “pied-à-terre”, or in layman’s terms “Second Home” tax have been notified. In this post, let’s look at the history of “pied-à-terre” taxes. What does this mean for New Yorkers? What are the logistics of this tax? Who really is affected by this, and how sustainable is this long-term? Examples of Pied-à-Terre Historically Let’s first define what pied-à-terre is. The term pied-à-terre is French for foot/feet on the ground. When it comes to how it applies to this tax, it is quite literally referring to a place of residence, usually located in metropolitan areas, and not used as an individual’s main living residence. For those wealthy enough to own more than one property, this causes a problem when it comes to housing supply. Legislation began to be discussed in the 2010s in Paris and New York, when taxes were starting to be discussed. In 2019, the first proposed bill that would have placed a recurring tax on luxury pieds-à-terre was blocked by real estate developers and lobbyists looking to protect them. On Tax Day this year (April 15th, 2026), the Governor of New York, Kathy Hochul, and New York Mayor, Zohran Mamdani, proposed a new version of the tax. The tax would apply to second homes valued at over $5 million. On May 27th, 2026, the New York State Legislature approved the tax. It took effect on July 1st, 2026. French Example With the term pied-à-terre being French, there is a prime example of the French government implementing rules to focus on the housing supply crisis that faced their residents. They had small apartments that were roughly 8 square meters, or for our American readers, 86 square feet. Not a lot of room, but they were sold or rented to people who needed them for work or for study rooms. In 2010, the French government instituted a rule that any French city with more than 200,000 inhabitants would require a minimum one-year lease on apartments. This is one way they have combated short-term rentals that would not be used. Netherlands Example While the French and Americans have higher-profile stories when it comes to pied-à-terre, the Netherlands have their own version. In Amsterdam, they define pied-à-terre based on a certain rental value. Additionally, they have the rule that if an owner of the house has their children living there, then every child needs to be registered within that municipality. It is common that many public figures in Amsterdam have their pied-à-terre in Amsterdam and live in other places. Benefits of the Pied-à-Terre tax One of the big talking points of the pied-à-terre tax is the revenue that would be brought in. The Governor and the Mayor estimate $500 million from roughly 13,000 homes that fall under the term pied-à-terre. These are the homes that have a market value of at least $5 million. Logistics of the tax There are many intricacies when it comes to who gets taxed and how much. To learn more about what the Comptroller’s website has laid out how they are going to implement this tax. This includes exemptions, tax rates, and even experience data based on how this shook out in Vancouver, England. What the estimated revenues need to take into account is the properties that are currently being rented. Those would not be subject to the tax. If this tax doesn’t yield the financial benefits that it is expected, the hope would be that enough housing opens up and more apartments would be available to purchase or rent. Below is a chart that shows how the surcharges will be applied: For property tax years 2026-27 and 2027-28, the surcharge will generally apply as follows: Property type DOF market value Surcharge rate (% of market value) One-, two-, and three-family homes $5,000,000 or greater, but less than $15,000,000 0.8% $15,000,000 or greater, but less than $25,000,000 1.05% $25,000,000 or greater 1.3% Condominium and cooperative units $1,000,000 or greater, but less than $3,000,000 4.0% $3,000,000 or greater, but less than $5,000,000 5.25% $5,000,000 or greater 6.50% Opposition to Pied-à-Terre tax When it comes to any taxes, it’s understandable that people want to protect their financial interests. One controversy that occurred with the notification of the property owners who would be subject to the second home tax, was the publication of the names and addresses associated with the tax. City officials have been clear that this happens twice a year for a public audit. The timing of the tax going into effect around the same time, of course, raised ears for those people who are sensitive to the nature of higher taxes. One critique of the tax boils down to the fact that market value defined by the city does not always correlate with actual worth. City officials have heard this complaint and will work to develop a new valuation system for the tax when it goes into effect in 2028. Exemptions Those who feel that they are not deserving of the city valuation can file for an exemption . Those in Residential homes, condos, and cooperative units have until September 18th, 2026 to file for an exemption. If you are the owner of the property, a tenant or subtenant, an individual who collectively holds a majority interest in the LLC, corporation, or partnership that owns the property, an immediate family member of the property owner, or the sole beneficiary or beneficiaries of a trust, you should be exempt from the surcharge. Just make sure you have the following documents: Primary residence documents All owners applying for an exemption from the surcharge will be asked to provide one of the following for each occupant you identify as using the property as a primary residence: Most recently filed federal or state tax return Driver’s license or other DMV-issued identification If a tax return, driver’s license, or other DMV-issued identification is not available, you can provide both of the following items: Voter identification card Other proof showing that the property is your primary residence Tenant documents If the property is the primary residence of a tenant or subtenant, you will be asked to provide the primary residence documents listed above, as well as: A copy of the current lease and one additional rental document, such as a utility bill, proof of rent payment, or renter’s insurance policy, OR A Tenant or Subtenant Affidavit and two additional rental documents Immediate family member If the property is the primary residence of an immediate family member of the owner or majority interest holder, you will be asked to provide the primary residence documents listed above, as well documentation proving the family relationship. Birth certificate Marriage certificate Immediate Family Member Affidavit Form Business entity If the property is owned by a business entity (such as an LLC, corporation, trust, or partnership) and is used as a primary residence by a majority member, shareholder, or partner, you will be asked to provide the primary residence documents listed above. In addition, you must provide: Partnership agreement, trust agreement or affidavit, LLC operating agreement, or articles of incorporation Majority Interest Affidavit The post What to Know About the New Pied-à-Terre Tax appeared first on Real Estate Topics, Tips, and Guides .

title: Best Digimind Alternatives Now That It's Onclusive Social
summary: Digimind rebranded to Onclusive Social in 2024. See how its pricing stacks up and find the right Digimind alternative for your budget-conscious enterprise team.
body_text: TL;DR: Digimind, the 27-year-old French social listening platform many enterprise teams still search for by name, no longer exists as a standalone product — Onclusive acquired it in 2022 and fully rebranded it "Onclusive Social" on October 29, 2024, with digimind.com now redirecting entirely to onclusive.com. If you're comparing Digimind alternatives for a budget-conscious enterprise team in 2026, the real fork in the road is buying process, not just price: Sprout Social and Hootsuite offer genuinely self-serve, published pricing you can start today, while Onclusive Social, Talkwalker, Meltwater, Brandwatch, and Syncly Social all compete at the enterprise-quote tier — where Onclusive Social's ~€15,000/year floor is the cheapest entry point, but the sales-gated buying experience is identical to its pricier peers. If you searched for "Digimind pricing" this year and landed on a page that says "Onclusive Social," you're not lost. You're just catching up to a rebrand that quietly finished more than a year ago. That's the uncomfortable starting point for anyone evaluating Digimind in 2026: the product is real, the reviews are good, and the company you're actually about to buy from doesn't go by that name anymore. Onclusive — backed by Symphony Technology Group — acquired Digimind in mid-2022, ran it under a "Digimind, an Onclusive company" co-brand for a couple of years, then folded it fully into "Onclusive Social" in October 2024. Trade press has since reported that the legacy digimind.com marketing site is set to close entirely around March 2026. None of that makes Digimind a bad tool. It's a genuinely credible, well-reviewed platform with real customers and a real AI feature. But it does mean a "Digimind alternatives" search in 2026 is really two searches at once: teams who assumed the product still existed under that name, and teams who knew about the rebrand and are now asking whether Onclusive Social's lower enterprise price point is actually more budget-friendly — or just a smaller number attached to the same demo-gated sales process as everyone else. This guide covers both, plus the video and audio coverage question that decides whether any of these tools can actually see what your customers are saying about you on TikTok. Why Do Budget-Conscious Enterprise Teams Look for Digimind Alternatives? The single biggest reason teams go looking for a Digimind alternative in 2026 isn't price — it's that "Digimind" has largely stopped existing as a distinct brand, and that identity churn creates real evaluation risk before budget even enters the conversation. The rebrand timeline, precisely: Digimind was founded in 1998 in Grenoble, France, and built a genuine 27-year track record in social listening and consumer intelligence before Onclusive announced its acquisition on July 25, 2022 (Source: Research Live, 2022 ). A lighter "Digimind, an Onclusive company" co-branding followed — it's still the name on Digimind's current G2 seller page — before Onclusive announced the full integration and rename to "Onclusive Social" on October 29, 2024 (Source: Media OutReach via Taiwan News, 2024 ). Today, digimind.com redirects entirely to onclusive.com, and trade press has reported the legacy marketing domain is scheduled to close around March 19, 2026 — a specific date that recurred consistently across search results this year but couldn't be traced to a single, independently fetchable primary source, so treat it as reported rather than confirmed. That two-stage timeline matters because most quick searches collapse it into one date or miss it entirely — which means a team that "evaluated Digimind six months ago" may already be evaluating a product that no longer carries that name. The second, more familiar reason is pricing opacity that persists despite a comparatively low entry point. Onclusive Social's starting price is consistently estimated at around €15,000 per year across third-party sources — genuinely lower than Brandwatch, Sprinklr, or Talkwalker's higher enterprise tiers (Source: Capterra, 2026 ). But there's still no published rate card, no self-serve checkout, and every path to a number runs through a sales conversation (Source: TrustRadius, 2026 ). Reviewer sentiment is genuinely mixed on top of that: aggregated G2 and Capterra reviews praise the platform's sentiment analysis and reporting depth, but also describe "extremely late deliverables" and, in one case, support that's "almost worthless" (Source: Capterra, 2026 ). How Does Digimind Pricing Compare to Its Alternatives? Onclusive Social sits at the budget end of the enterprise-quote tier, not in genuinely self-serve territory — its ~€15,000/year floor undercuts Brandwatch and Talkwalker's higher tiers, but the buying experience is identical to theirs: no published pricing, no self-serve checkout, demo required just to see a number. Quote-only pricing : A vendor pricing model where no rate card is published publicly and every quote requires a sales conversation, regardless of how large or small the deal is. That's the tension worth sitting with before you get attached to Digimind's lower absolute number. A team optimizing purely to avoid a multi-month enterprise sales cycle will find Sprout Social or Hootsuite meaningfully more accessible, even though Onclusive Social's ceiling may end up cheaper once you're actually in a contract. Tool Best For Starting Price Self-Serve? Video/Audio Capability Syncly Social Video-native brand and consumer-insights teams Custom (free trial available) Yes (trial) Native — audio transcription + on-screen visual detection, all tiers Digimind (Onclusive Social) Budget end of enterprise-tier listening ~€15,000/yr (quote-only) No 2018-era static-image logo recognition (unconfirmed today) — no video/speech Sprout Social Genuinely self-serve listening + management $79/seat/mo Yes None confirmed — caption/keyword only Hootsuite Most accessible self-serve entry point $99–$249/user/mo (source-dependent) Yes (30-day trial) Unconfirmed for the Listening tier specifically Talkwalker Enterprise breadth + real video/audio AI ~$9,000–$13,000/yr (Core) No Non-gated speech-to-text + video-logo recognition, all tiers Meltwater PR + social intelligence with shipped video transcription ~$6,000/yr (Starter) No Genuine TikTok/YouTube/Instagram video transcription Brandwatch Deepest historical consumer-intelligence archive Custom (enterprise) No Roadmapped, not shipped A few things worth calling out in that table. Talkwalker's entry-level Core tier can actually start below Digimind's own floor while shipping meaningfully more capability. Meltwater's Starter tier is priced closer to a mid-market tool than an enterprise one, even though it competes for the same category of deal. And Sprout Social and Hootsuite are the only two vendors here you could plausibly be live on by the end of the week — no quote, no demo, just a credit card and a trial. Which Digimind Alternatives Cover Video and Audio Content, Not Just Text? Only two vendors in this comparison — Talkwalker and Meltwater — ship confirmed, non-gated video and audio capability; Onclusive Social's 2018-era "AI Sense" image-recognition feature is real but no longer confirmed by current product marketing, and video or audio content analysis in any form is absent from its current pitch — putting it in the same ceiling as Sprout Social, Hootsuite, and Brandwatch. This is the honest, easy-to-overstate-or-understate part of the story, so it's worth being precise. Digimind's own data scientists built a genuine AI layer called "AI Sense" back in 2018, working with IBM Research, using deep learning to detect brand logos inside images (Source: PRWeb, 2018 ). That's a real, independently developed capability — not a "dumb keyword tool" claim. But Onclusive's current product page has moved the "AI Sense" name onto different ground: it now describes a real-time sentiment engine that powers a summarization feature ("In Brief") and an alerting feature ("Sentinel"), with no mention of logo detection, image recognition, speech-to-text, audio transcription, or motion-video analysis anywhere on it (Source: Onclusive, 2026 ). Whether the original image-recognition layer is still live under the hood isn't something current marketing confirms either way — what is confirmed is that video and audio content analysis, in any form, isn't part of the current pitch. An independent third-party comparison backs that reading: "Neither platform offers complete TikTok analytics integration," referring to Digimind and Hootsuite alike (Source: Mention, 2025 ). Text/mention-matching listening : Monitoring that scans captions, hashtags, and platform metadata for keyword or mention matches — it can't hear what's said out loud in a video or see what's shown on screen. Video-content-native listening : Monitoring that processes the actual audio and visual content of a video — transcribing spoken words and detecting on-screen text, logos, or visual cues — surfacing mentions even when the caption and hashtags say nothing about your brand. By that definition, Onclusive Social, Sprout Social, and Hootsuite are all text/mention-matching tools at their core, with Onclusive Social's 2018-era static-image logo detection layered on top as a genuine but now-unconfirmed exception — it doesn't appear anywhere in current Onclusive product marketing. Brandwatch has publicly roadmapped deeper video and image analysis but hasn't shipped it. Talkwalker and Meltwater are the two enterprise peers that have actually shipped video-content-native listening — non-gated speech-to-text and video-logo recognition in Talkwalker's case, and real TikTok, YouTube, and Instagram transcription in Meltwater's. Syncly Social was built video-native from the start specifically to close this gap, with video analysis and audio transcription running by default rather than as an upsell. That gap matters more than it used to. Health and beauty alone now accounts for 79.3% of TikTok Shop sales, generating more than $1.34 billion annually (Source: BeautyMatter, 2025 ) — a category where a growing share of brand-relevant conversation happens in spoken video or on-screen visuals a caption-matching tool simply never sees. Which Digimind Alternative Fits a Budget-Conscious Enterprise Team? "Budget-conscious enterprise team" isn't one buyer profile — it splits into teams that want the lowest number within the enterprise-quote tier, and teams that want to skip the quote-gated sales process altogether, and the right alternative depends on which one you actually are. 1. Syncly Social Syncly Social is built for teams whose customers talk about them out loud or show them on-screen inside TikTok, Instagram Reels, or YouTube Shorts — conversation that Onclusive Social's image-only AI was never built to detect, and that neither Sprout Social nor Hootsuite catch either. Audio Intelligence (speech-to-text) and AI Vision (on-screen text and logo detection) run natively across video content, not scoped down to static images. Pricing is custom, but the path in is a genuine free trial rather than a demo-only gate — a meaningfully different buying experience from every enterprise-tier vendor on this list, including Onclusive Social itself. It's the strongest fit if your evaluation criteria include real social listening coverage of video content specifically, alongside competitor analysis that doesn't stop at what competitors caption. 2. Sprout Social Sprout Social is the most accessible buying process in this entire comparison: published, self-serve pricing from $79/seat/month up through $399/seat/month, with Enterprise the only custom tier (Source: Sprout Social, 2026 ). No demo required to start. The honest trade-off is that it's confirmed keyword, hashtag, and caption-only listening — Sprout's own documentation states it "cannot search and sync sound" on TikTok (Source: Sprout Social Support, 2026 ) — meaning it gives up even Onclusive Social's narrow image-recognition layer in exchange for a fully self-serve buying process. 3. Hootsuite Hootsuite is the other genuinely self-serve option, with published tiers generally cited between $99 and $399 per user per month, though a live Capterra comparison widget lists it closer to $249/user/month — likely reflecting different plan tiers being surfaced (Source: Capterra, 2026 ). Its listening layer is now "powered by Talkwalker" following Hootsuite's 2024 acquisition of that company (Source: Hootsuite Newsroom, 2024 ), but no source confirms whether Talkwalker's video and audio AI is actually exposed inside Hootsuite's own listening tier — an open question worth asking directly in a sales call rather than assuming either way. 4. Brandwatch Brandwatch competes on depth rather than price: a historical archive stretching back to 2010 and enterprise-grade consumer-research tooling, at a custom price point generally comparable to or above Onclusive Social's floor. Its 2026 roadmap lists deeper video and image analysis as a stated goal, not a shipped feature — so paying more than Onclusive Social's floor for Brandwatch today doesn't automatically buy more video coverage. 5. Talkwalker Talkwalker is the strongest "spend about the same, get real video AI" case in this comparison. Third-party estimates put its entry-level Core tier at roughly $9,000 to $13,000 per year — potentially below Onclusive Social's own floor — while shipping non-gated speech-to-text and video-logo recognition on every tier, not just the top one. The trade-off is a steeper learning curve than Onclusive Social's reviewer-praised ease of use, and marketing copy that describes its video capability generically rather than confirming platform-specific depth on TikTok or Reels. 6. Meltwater Meltwater combines PR and social intelligence with genuine, already-shipped TikTok, YouTube, and Instagram video transcription through its TikTok Marketing Partners integration — a real step up from Onclusive Social's image-only AI. Pricing is quote-based, with analyst estimates ranging from roughly $6,000 at the Starter tier to $150,000-plus at Enterprise, median around $15,000–$25,000 per year (Source: Vendr, 2026 ). Named customers include Shiseido , Yves Rocher , and Bon Parfumeur (Source: Meltwater customer stories, 2026). For a wider view of how enterprise listening vendors stack up on price and video coverage more broadly, see how NetBase Quid's alternatives compare or how Sprinklr, Sprout Social, and Agorapulse fit different budgets . Key Takeaways Digimind no longer exists as a standalone brand — Onclusive acquired it in 2022 and fully rebranded it "Onclusive Social" on October 29, 2024, with digimind.com now redirecting to onclusive.com. A reported March 2026 domain closure is trade-press-sourced, not independently confirmed. Onclusive Social's ~€15,000/year starting price is the cheapest entry point among the enterprise-quote vendors here, but it's still quote-only with no self-serve checkout — the same buying friction as Brandwatch or Talkwalker. Sprout Social ($79/seat/mo) and Hootsuite ($99–$249/user/mo) are the only genuinely self-serve alternatives — no demo required to start. Onclusive Social's "AI Sense" began in 2018 as a real, IBM Research-developed static-image logo detector, but current Onclusive product marketing doesn't reference it — and confirms no speech or video content analysis either way. Talkwalker and Meltwater are the two vendors here with confirmed, shipped video/audio AI. "Budget-conscious enterprise team" splits into two buyers: those chasing the lowest number within the enterprise-quote tier, and those who want to skip the sales-gated process entirely — the right alternative depends on which one you are. The Verdict Digimind was never a bad tool — it's a credible, well-reviewed platform that simply doesn't exist under that name anymore, and its successor's lower enterprise price tag doesn't change the fact that you still can't see a number without a sales call. If cost accessibility means "avoid the demo cycle," Sprout Social or Hootsuite will get you live faster than anything else on this list. If it means "get enterprise breadth for less," Talkwalker's Core tier and Meltwater's Starter pricing are worth a direct comparison against Onclusive Social's floor. And if your actual problem is that customers are talking about you on camera rather than in captions, none of the text-first options — Onclusive Social included — were built to hear them. title: IDIQ Task Order Proposal Tips for Large Contractors (August 2026)
summary: This August 2026 guide covers task order proposal strategy for IDIQ holders: bid/no-bid calls, pricing, compliance matrices, and review models.
body_text: Most IDIQ task order proposal strategy advice focuses on writing better. That's the wrong starting point. By the time your team is writing, the firms with strong agency relationships and pre-positioned content are already three steps ahead. Getting competitive on a multiple-award vehicle is a pre-RFP problem as much as a proposal problem. TLDR: Holding an IDIQ seat generates no revenue; your win rate at the task order level determines portfolio value. Make bid/no-bid calls within 24 hours of release, weighting customer intimacy most heavily over technical fit. Read the ordering guide before every response: evaluation methodology, page limits, and pricing structures vary by order and by vehicle. Use FOIA requests on prior awarded orders to anchor pricing on orders above $1 million, where internal estimates often miss the competitive range. Proposal automation tools that parse PWS and Section L/M requirements into a compliance matrix and annotated outline before writing begins have documented results including 3-4x faster proposal preparation and 80% reduction in SME time on early-stage proposals. The Competitive Reality of Multiple-Award IDIQ Task Orders Holding a seat on a multiple-award IDIQ vehicle does not generate revenue. Winning task orders does. That distinction shapes everything about how high-performing contractors approach their IDIQ portfolios, and it is where most firms underinvest. The competitive pressure at the task order level is concentrated in ways that open-market proposals are not. You are competing against a known, finite set of vehicle holders, often anywhere from 3 to 15 awardees per order, all of whom cleared the same qualification bar you did. The government has already vetted everyone at the table. What separates winners from the rest is execution speed, proposal discipline, and how well a team has positioned itself before the task order RFP ever drops. Federal agencies obligate billions annually through IDIQ vehicles , making task order competition one of the highest-volume, highest-stakes arenas in federal contracting. The volume itself creates the pressure: orders come fast, turnaround windows are tight, and agencies have little tolerance for proposals that miss requirements or read like recycled boilerplate from the master contract response. The firms that build repeatable task order proposal processes pull ahead quickly. Those that treat each order as a one-off scramble tend to win inconsistently, regardless of their technical capability. Chevo , a mid-sized federal contractor managing multiple active vehicles, cut proposal prep time by 30-40% after systematizing their response workflow with GovEagle, a concrete illustration of what repeatable process infrastructure looks like in practice. Building a Task Order Bid/No-Bid Framework Task order bid/no-bid decisions fail when they get treated like open-market ones. The review committee, the deliberation, the 48-hour conversation: none of that fits a vehicle where the window from release to response can be five days or fewer. If your team hasn't made the call within 24 hours of release, you're already behind. Three variables should drive the decision: Customer relationship and intimacy: Has your team engaged this program office before the RFP dropped? Do you have a named point of contact, a prior task order, or documented past performance on this work? Competitive positioning among co-holders: Of the other vehicle holders, how many have stronger incumbent positioning or a more direct capability match? If you're facing two incumbent-adjacent firms and you have no prior relationship with the ordering activity, the math is hard. Internal resource availability: Can you staff this without pulling critical personnel off active delivery or a higher-priority pursuit? Decision Variable Strong Signal (Bid) Weak Signal (No-Bid) Customer Relationship & Intimacy Named POC, prior task order, or documented past performance on this work No prior agency engagement; ordering activity is unfamiliar Competitive Positioning Among Co-Holders No incumbent-adjacent firms; direct capability match to the PWS Two or more co-holders with stronger incumbent positioning Internal Resource Availability Key personnel available without pulling from active delivery Pursuit would strain capacity on higher-priority orders Teams managing three or more vehicles simultaneously can't afford to rebuild this framework every time an order drops. The answer is a standing decision gate: a one-page scoring card with weighted criteria that a single BD lead can complete in under an hour. Weight customer intimacy most heavily; it predicts win probability at the task order level more reliably than technical capability alone, because the agency already confirmed your technical baseline when it awarded you a seat. The gate should also include a hard stop: if two of the three variables score below threshold, the default is no-bid. Selective pursuit improves average proposal quality and protects your team's capacity for the orders where your positioning is genuinely strong. Pre-RFP Positioning at the Task Order Level The window that determines a task order's outcome often closes before the RFTOP is published. Ordering agencies signal demand through program reviews, budget documentation, and informal outreach to vehicle holders they already trust. Teams that track those signals hold a structural head start. A few concrete practices make the difference: Monitor vehicle-specific portals and the ordering agency's forecast data for upcoming task requirements and funding timelines. Map the agency's historical task-release cadence so your team can anticipate heavy response periods and staff accordingly. Submit white papers or attend industry days tied to specific program offices, creating a record of engagement that precedes the formal solicitation. Pre-slot key personnel against the roles most likely to appear in the PWS before any order drops. The best task order proposals are written before the RFP releases. By the time the clock starts, the technical approach should already exist in draft form. Capture plan intelligence gathered here needs a place to live. Notes trapped in a BD lead's inbox don't reach the proposal team when it matters. The teams that win consistently have a system that connects pre-RFP agency context directly to the response workspace, so writers aren't reconstructing what the capture lead already knew. Writing a Compliant, Tailored Task Order Technical Volume Evaluators on a vehicle ordering activity have typically reviewed dozens of responses against the same PWS structure. Recycled boilerplate reads as exactly that, and it signals a team that did not engage with the specific requirement. The starting move is a direct PWS-to-proposal mapping: list every task area in the statement of work, then assign each a corresponding proposal section. Any task area without a mapped response is a compliance gap. Do that mapping before writing begins, not after a draft exists. Past performance citation is where teams lose the most time. Searching after RFP release costs hours; a pre-indexed content library organized by PWS task domain, contract value, and agency lets you surface relevant references in minutes. Pull three to five that match the specific work mix in this order, not your strongest references overall. Win themes belong in the technical volume, but page constraints mean every sentence has to carry weight. Integrate discriminators into the methodology description instead of appending a separate "why us" paragraph. If a discriminator cannot be woven into a specific task area response, it probably does not belong in the volume at all. Measuring and Improving Task Order Win Rates Aggregate task order win rate is a vanity metric. A 40% win rate looks reasonable until you break it down and find you're winning 70% on one vehicle and 15% on another. The signal lives in the segmentation: win rate by vehicle, by ordering agency, by evaluation methodology, and by order size tier. Post-award debriefings are the most underused diagnostic tool available. FAR 16.505(b)(6) gives you the right to request one on any order above $7.5 million. Most teams skip it, which closes off the most direct feedback loop available. Evaluator notes on a lost order often reveal structural proposal weaknesses that internal red team reviews miss entirely. Three metrics worth tracking at the vehicle portfolio level: Win rate by vehicle and ordering agency, segmented by evaluation methodology (best-value vs. LPTA), so you can isolate where your approach is actually working Proposal throughput measured as orders bid versus orders available against BD capacity consumed, which surfaces whether you are spreading pursuit resources too thin Revenue yield per vehicle, calculated as total task order value awarded relative to BD hours invested, which identifies which vehicles deserve deeper pursuit investment That last metric is where most IDIQ holders find the clearest decision point. A vehicle where you hold a seat but have won nothing in 18 months warrants a hard look before the next order drops. How GovEagle Accelerates Task Order Response for IDIQ Holders The process gaps described throughout this article (late bid/no-bid calls, disconnected capture intelligence, compressed review cycles) share a common structural cause: proposal teams rebuilding from scratch on every order instead of executing against pre-positioned infrastructure. GovEagle closes that gap directly. It parses task order PWS and Section L/M requirements into a compliance matrix generated natively in Excel, then produces an annotated proposal outline in Microsoft Word before writing begins. That sequence, RFP parsing through compliant structure, is where most turnaround windows collapse under manual approaches. Integrity Defense Solutions achieved 3 to 4 times faster proposal preparation using GovEagle, and Chevo cut RFI response time by 30 to 40 percent. Precise Software reduced SME time on early-stage proposals by 80 percent, which is the capacity headroom that makes higher task order bid volume sustainable without adding headcount. For vehicles like OASIS+ Phase II, where GSA issues amendments on a rolling basis, GovEagle's amendment tracking automatically identifies solicitation changes and updates the compliance matrix and annotated outline accordingly. A single untracked amendment can misalign an otherwise strong response. GovEagle connects capture intelligence, compliance documentation, and proposal execution in one traceable system: not a point tool for any single phase, but the workflow infrastructure that supports the proposal factory model end to end. FAQs How do I structure a task order technical volume when the ordering guide hasn't disclosed evaluation factors? Start with a direct PWS-to-proposal mapping: list every task area in the statement of work and assign each a corresponding proposal section before writing begins, so any unmapped task area registers as a compliance gap immediately. Final Thoughts on Competing Effectively at the IDIQ Task Order Level Most of what separates high task order win rates from inconsistent ones isn't visible in the proposal itself. title: The cursed hot potato of B2B event management | Zuddl Blog
summary: In B2B event management, when things break, they break in front of executives and top prospects. Here is why blame always lands on the event marketer.
body_text: There are two ways things go wrong in marketing. The first way is quieter. An email campaign underperforms, or an ad sequence misses its targets. You spot them in dashboards and they might be reviewed in a meeting. There's time to adjust and try again. The second way happens in front of your CMO, your sales team, your best prospects, and maybe even your CEO. That's events. Picture this: it's 8:40 AM. Doors open in twenty minutes. The check-in queue is a mile long. Three senior executives from a key account are standing near the entrance, watching the line not move. Your phone starts blowing up. Catch! That’s your event hot potato now. It doesn’t matter if you didn't build the platform or choose the architecture direction. You just happened to be there. “It feels like a lot of the blame was [on us] and there hasn't been a lot on [the vendor] to help resolve or make sure this isn't going to happen again”, said a senior marketing ops director after a live stream went down during an event. Nobody's thinking bout API integration. If a session link breaks and a speaker panics twelve minutes before go-live, the platform is far from their minds. Who else do they turn to but you? The problem is, most of the causes for these issues are not in the event marketer's control. What B2B event management platforms were built for (and where they fall short) The first generation of event management software was built for logistics challenges: process registrations, print badges, send emails, export a spreadsheet at the end. Platforms made themselves transactional and got good at moving people through a funnel. Every one of those functions generates data. The check-in slowdown is visible in the system, but nothing alerts the events team. A corrupt session link might stay broken for days, but nothing flags it before go-live. When a lead engages with three sessions and then goes cold, the event platform probably doesn't have enough context to tell you that. Hunting for the right signal can feel like using a telescope to look for ants Most event tech didn't get built end to end. Companies running multiple event types have had to run one tool for conferences and a different one for webinars, and none of these share data. A brand kit configured in one doesn't carry into the next. You end up with a tacked together workflow running via spreadhseets. There's a manual reconciliation round with every new event. Those are the cracks you fall through. Because you hold all the context for the event, you become the real-time warning system that continuously monitors for problems and coordinates manual handoffs, on top of everything else an event demands. The responsibility that doesn't come with line of sight The irony of running an event program is that it is measured against how much pipeline it influences, but the parts that are crucial to the pipeline don't belong to the events function. The CRM belongs to marketing ops. Post-event follow up is under sales. The data routing that decides whether a hot lead gets called the same afternoon or five days later is a platform decision that's out of everyone's control. These dependencies make it slower to get to the outcome. Since the running of an event is spread across multiple teams, you get functional siloes that make it hard to share context with everyone. [.ebook-q-card][.ebook-body-text] According to a Forrester study, only one in five enterprises has integrated their primary event platform with their wider marketing technology stack. [.ebook-body-text][.ebook-q-card] These siloes also lead to event tech being seen as a tactical asset focused on running the event rather than a way to strategically power the whole program. This broken system has been normalized for far too long. For an event program to really work, the marketer needs to have visibility across the whole chain. Only then can they spot the gaps and fix them proactively instead of always putting out fires. The platform escaped accountability it should have owned Let's go back to the 8:40 AM scene at the start, but now as you position yourself to catch the hot potato, you step aside and let it land on the box that's marked 'tooling'. Because now you know that the question isn't about people or preparation. It is information. Dodge the hot potatoes with the right platform A platform that's built for an event marketer should be able to surface problems before you go live. It should run QA on your event before you publish, route leads automatically the moment someone badges in , and escalate when a rep misses the follow-up window. It should allow you to run on-brand events fast without having to depend on multiple teams. That can only work when these features can access the same record and know that a badge scan happened, that QA flagged a broken link, and that a rep's SLA clock is running. Visibility across the chain shouldn't take more effort from you. That's the vent platform's responsibility. That's the difference between catching the hot potato and turning it into fries.

title: What Legal Talent Teams Are Already Doing With AI
summary: Law firm talent leaders are asking: what does AI actually change about our work now, not in five years?
body_text: Law firm talent leaders are asking: what does AI actually change about our work now, not in five years? The technology matters less than what a team does with it. Over the past few months we released a set of AI capabilities across Flo Applicant Tracking and Flo Performance Management, plus Flo AI reporting on top of both, and it’s been thrilling to Flo to see what firms have done with them: a candidate database that holds up under scrutiny, performance reviews that deliver superior feedback, answers to questions that used to require a spreadsheet and a free afternoon, and a resume parser that actually works. Here’s what our recent updates look like in action for Flo clients. A candidate database your recruiting team can trust Candidates enter a database through direct applications, events, agency submissions, and manual adds. Any of those paths can create a second record for someone already in the system, and fragmented history makes a candidate's status harder to trust when it matters most. In agency-driven lateral recruiting, that is a financial problem as much as an operational one. Unclear candidate ownership is how fee disputes start. Flo now scans the candidate list with the most advanced automated matching on the market and flags clusters of records that appear to represent the same person, rather than relying on any single, exact field match. Opening "Manage Duplicates" shows each cluster, the records inside it, and whether agency submissions are involved. Merging produces one authoritative record, and all agency submission history survives the merge, which is the point: firms need to know which agency submitted whom long after two entries were combined. If a cluster turns out to be two different people, dismissing it keeps them separate going forward. The duplicate problem gets caught as it arises rather than when it’s too late to avoid a fee dispute. High quality feedback that reflects what the reviewer meant Performance reviews shape how an attorney is perceived, developed, and advanced. The writing is hard. A comment can land harsher or vaguer than intended, and coded language can slip in unnoticed before a review is published. Reading every comment for tone manually has never been realistic at scale. Two capabilities in Flo Performance Management now sit with the reviewer, in the moment. AI Rewrite allows partners and managers to paste messy notes or jot down stream of consciousness thoughts in their review form and turn them into a cohesive, polished review. AI Rewrite provides readily available prompt options like “more concise” and “more direct,” plus allows for custom instructions for the rewrite. Rewrite works only from review content already entered, never adding in examples or details that were not originally written. The substance stays with the human. AI Tone Assist helps reviewers deliver high quality and appropriate feedback by 1) highlighting phrases that may read as vague or problematic, 2) providing an explanation, and 3) suggesting a correction, like that the reviewer add specific examples or replace a certain word. It flags gendered or coded language applied unevenly across groups, references to protected characteristics, vague feedback with no supporting example, unprofessional language, and overused HR clichés. Flags are informational, and Tone Assist never blocks a submission. Reviewers get a chance to self-correct before feedback reaches a reviewee or enters a formal record. Professional development and HR teams get a consistent standard applied across reviews without depending on manual oversight alone. Questions that used to take weeks to answer – that firm leadership needs answers to now Which recruiting sources produce the associates who go on to perform the highest? How do themes in performance reviews affect our recruiting strategy? Which interviewers consistently predict a top performer? Firm leaders have carried questions like these for years without a practical way to answer them, because the answer lives in two systems that never talked to each other. Flo AI reporting answers them in plain language, from a firm's own recruiting and performance data, across Flo Pipeline Building, Applicant Tracking, Work Allocation, and Performance Management. A practice group head opening a senior litigation associate search can ask which qualifications predicted strong hires in past litigation searches and which candidates in the current pipeline match. A talent leader can ask which skills and backgrounds now predict the firm's highest performers, and how that has shifted over the past few years, reading interview evaluations and performance reviews together. That second question is the one that was previously out of reach. Spreadsheets handle structured data, and the most useful signal in talent work sits in the unstructured text of feedback forms, evaluations, and notes. Flo AI reporting reads that text at scale and points to the candidates, reviews, and matters behind every answer, so a leader can check the reasoning rather than take the number on faith. Decisions about who to hire and how to develop them now rest on a firm's full record rather than whatever could be exported into a spreadsheet before the meeting. Resume parsing that actually works Resume parsing is table stakes for an applicant tracking system, yet has a reputation for low quality results. Most teams have used a version of it that dropped a job title into the school field, mangled anything with two columns, and left the candidate correcting the form rather than filling it out. Table stakes only counts if the feature works, and for years this one mostly did not. AI changed what is possible here. Parsing is now live on the candidate-facing career page, in the agency portal, and on the admin job details page. A candidate or agency representative uploads a resume, and in about 10 seconds the application fills in bio data, education history, and work history, accurately enough to leave alone. The parser does not touch self-identification fields or application-specific questions, which stay deliberate. The uploaded file attaches itself to the resume section, so nobody finishes a form and then goes looking for the document again. Lateral candidates – and their agency recruiters – are employed, busy, and evaluating an opportunity carefully. Retyping a work history that already sits in a document on their desktop was never a good use of that attention. For agencies submitting on a firm's behalf, the effect compounds, because every manual field was a place for a typo, a delay, or a drop-off. Teams are seeing more complete applications arrive with less back-and-forth to correct them. The common thread None of these features make the decision. The parser does not fill in self-identification fields. Duplicate detection surfaces clusters and leaves the merge to an admin. Rewrite will not invent a fact a reviewer did not observe. Tone Assist flags and explains, then gets out of the way. Flo AI reporting shows its work and leaves hiring, promotion, and development calls with the people accountable for them. That is deliberate. In legal talent work, judgment is the job, and the useful role for AI is removing the friction around it. Each of these came out of clients telling us what they were running into. Tell us what you hit next. Want to see these in action? Book a demo and we will walk you through them. Flo AI meets the highest security and data privacy standards of law firms. Learn about our AI security .

body_text: PDF Version SEOUL, South Korea, Aug. 11, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- DoubleDown Interactive Co., Ltd. (NASDAQ: DDI) (“DoubleDown” or the “Company”), a leading developer and publisher of digital games on mobile and web-based platforms, today announced unaudited financial results for the second quarter ended June 30, 2026. Second Quarter 2026 vs. Second Quarter 2025 Summary: Revenue rose 11.2% to $94.3 million in the second quarter of 2026 compared to $84.8 million in the second quarter of 2025. Revenue from the Company’s social casino/free-to-play games was $77.3 million in the second quarter of 2026, an 11.5% increase from the second quarter of 2025. The increase was primarily due to contributions from WHOW Games GmbH (“WHOW Games”), which was acquired by the Company in July 2025. Direct-to-Consumer (“DTC”)1 revenue rose to $40.5 million in the second quarter of 2026, compared to $10.7 million in the second quarter of 2025. DTC revenue as a percentage of total social casino revenue increased to 52.4% in the second quarter of 2026 from 15.4% in the second quarter of 2025. Revenue from SuprNation, the Company’s iGaming subsidiary, increased 9.8% year over year to $17.0 million, primarily as a result of the continued success of the Company’s newest brand, Los Vegas . Operating expenses were $57.8 million in the second quarter of 2026 compared to $52.4 million in the second quarter of 2025, primarily due to the inclusion of operating expenses of WHOW Games. Profit for the interim period (excluding non-controlling interest) rose 50.5% to $32.9 million, or earnings per fully diluted common share of $13.27 ($0.66 per American Depositary Share (“ADS”)), in the second quarter of 2026, compared to $21.8 million, or earnings per fully diluted common share of $8.82 ($0.44 per ADS), in the second quarter of 2025. The increase was primarily due to higher revenue, higher unrealized gain on foreign currency, and lower cost of revenue attributable to a higher proportion of DTC revenue, partially offset by higher overall operating expenses, which were primarily due to the inclusion of WHOW Games, and increased costs to support SuprNation’s revenue growth. Each ADS represents 0.05 share of a common share. Adjusted EBITDA rose 17.2% to $39.3 million for the second quarter of 2026, compared to $33.5 million in the second quarter of 2025. Adjusted EBITDA margin increased to 41.6% in the second quarter of 2026, compared to 39.5% in the second quarter of 2025. Beginning in the fourth quarter of 2025, social casino KPIs are inclusive of those from WHOW Games. Payer Conversion ratio for the Company’s social casino/free-to-play games increased to 9.4% in the second quarter of 2026 from 7.0% in the second quarter of 2025, primarily as a result of the inclusion of WHOW Games, which has a higher Payer Conversion ratio. Average Revenue Per Daily Active User (“ARPDAU”) for the Company’s social casino/free-to-play games increased to $1.42 in the second quarter of 2026 from $1.33 in the second quarter of 2025, primarily as a result of the inclusion of WHOW Games, which has a higher ARPDAU. Average monthly revenue per payer for the social casino/free-to-play games decreased to $218 in the second quarter of 2026 from $286 in the second quarter of 2025, primarily as a result of the inclusion of WHOW Games, which has a lower average revenue per payer. Net cash flows from operating activities increased to $24.6 million in the second quarter of 2026 from $19.7 million in the second quarter of 2025. The increase is primarily due to lower income taxes paid. _____________________ 1 Direct-to-Consumer revenue represents revenue from purchases made through Company-owned channels, including web storefront transactions and other direct payment flows. "Our double-digit year-over-year revenue and adjusted EBITDA growth in the second quarter reflect our team’s continued focus on operational excellence," said In Keuk Kim, Chief Executive Officer of DoubleDown. "These strong quarterly results highlight ongoing growth in our Direct-to-Consumer segment, which now accounts for over 50% of total social casino revenue. Performance was driven by contributions from WHOW Games, solid growth in our core social casino business that we believe outpaced the broader market, and continued year-over-year momentum from SuprNation, our iGaming business, following the successful launch of our 'Los Vegas' brand. "Our ability to consistently drive a high conversion of revenue to cash flow remains a top operating priority, resulting in $24.6 million of net cash flow from operations in the second quarter and a total of $71.0 million for the first half of 2026. As we look to the second half of 2026, we are well positioned to build upon our success. With an aggregate net cash position of $521 million, DoubleDown's strong balance sheet provides us with substantial financial flexibility to pursue strategic growth opportunities as well as additional value-building initiatives and transactions for our shareholders."
